subject: system-design
title: API Design
summary: Design APIs that are clear, evolvable, safe to retry and hard to abuse: REST, GraphQL and gRPC, pagination, idempotency, rate limiting, auth, real-time and webhooks.

lessons.title: Resources and HTTP method contracts
lessons.summary: Model resources and distinguish safe, idempotent and partial-update operations.
lessons.body:
Almost every system design answer has a box labelled "API". Before you can argue about GraphQL, rate limits or idempotency keys, you need a precise model of what a plain HTTP API promises. REST gives you that model.

REST (Representational State Transfer) was described by Roy Fielding in his 2000 PhD dissertation. It isn't a protocol or a library. It's a set of constraints that, if you follow them, give you an API that caches well, scales horizontally and supports evolvability; application contracts and compatibility still require design.

## Resources, not actions

The central idea is the **resource**: a noun that has an identity and a URL. A customer, an order, a list of orders. Clients manipulate *representations* of resources (usually JSON) using a small, fixed set of verbs.

Compare two designs for the same feature:

```
RPC style         REST style
--------------    ---------------------
POST /getOrder    GET  /orders/42
POST /addOrder    POST /orders
POST /cancel      POST /orders/42/cancel
POST /listOrders  GET  /orders?status=open
```

The RPC style invents a new verb per operation. Every client has to learn each one, and the method alone does not advertise safe/idempotent operation semantics. Explicit response caching metadata can still make certain POST responses cacheable. In the REST style the verb carries meaning that the whole HTTP ecosystem understands.

> [!tip] Nouns in paths, verbs in methods
> Use plural nouns (`/orders`, `/orders/42/items`). When an action genuinely doesn't fit CRUD, such as cancelling or refunding, use a pragmatic action endpoint (`POST /orders/42/cancel`) or as a new resource (`POST /refunds`). Don't contort the domain to avoid it.

Keep nesting shallow. `/customers/7/orders/42` is fine; `/customers/7/orders/42/items/3/options/9` is a sign that `items` deserves its own top-level resource.

## HTTP methods: safe and idempotent

RFC 9110 defines two properties that matter enormously in distributed systems.

- **Safe**: the method is read-only in intent. The client is not asking for any state change. Crawlers, prefetchers and caches may call it freely.
- **Idempotent**: making the same request N times has the same effect on the server as making it once. The *response* may differ (a second `DELETE` may return 404), but the server's state ends up the same.

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | Yes | Yes | Read a resource |
| HEAD | Yes | Yes | Headers only |
| OPTIONS | Yes | Yes | CORS preflight |
| PUT | No | Yes | Replace whole resource |
| DELETE | No | Yes | Remove resource |
| PATCH | No | Not by default | Partial update |
| POST | No | No | Create, or run a process |

Every safe method is idempotent, but not the other way round. `DELETE /orders/42` changes state, yet doing it twice leaves the order deleted either way.

## Why idempotency matters

Networks fail in the worst possible place: *after* the server did the work but *before* the client got the response. The client sees a timeout and has no idea whether the request happened.

```
Client            Server
  |--- PUT x=5 ---->|
  |                 | writes x=5
  |    X<-- 200 ----|  (lost)
  | timeout!        |
  |--- PUT x=5 ---->|  retry: x=5
  |<--- 200 --------|  still x=5
```

With `PUT`, the retry is harmless. With `POST /payments`, a retry could charge the customer twice. That's why RFC 9110 lets clients and proxies retry idempotent requests automatically, and why clients need evidence that a non-idempotent operation is safe to retry or that the original was not applied; proxies must not automatically retry non-idempotent requests. Making `POST` safe to retry needs extra machinery (idempotency keys), covered later in this module.

## PUT vs PATCH

`PUT` requests replacement of the target resource state with the supplied representation. The API defines how writable fields map to state; server-managed fields and related resources need not be erased merely because they are absent. Repeating the same replacement has the same intended effect.

```
PUT /users/7
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com"}
```

`PATCH` sends a set of changes. A JSON Merge Patch like `{"email": "new@example.com"}` happens to be idempotent. A patch like "append item to list" or "increment counter" is not. So the HTTP spec doesn't promise `PATCH` is idempotent; your API might.

> [!warning] Don't change state on GET
> A `GET /users/7/delete` link will eventually be followed by a crawler, a link-preview bot or a browser prefetch. Teams have lost data this way. Safe means safe.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Setting a thermostat
> **How it maps:** Setting the target to 20 degrees repeatedly leaves the same target. Asking it to raise the target by one degree repeatedly keeps changing it. This mirrors absolute assignment versus an increment.
>
> **Where it stops:** Idempotency concerns the intended operation, not identical responses, logs or every physical side effect.

## Key takeaways
- Use resource identities and standard methods to make intent visible.
- Safe methods request no state change; incidental logging is allowed. Idempotent methods preserve the intended effect on repetition.
- PUT replaces writable resource state; PATCH idempotency depends on the changes requested.
- A timeout is an unknown outcome. Non-idempotent retries need evidence and an enforced contract.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
- [MDN: HTTP request methods](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods)

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is idempotent but **not** safe?

options.text: GET
options.explanation: GET is both safe and idempotent. It's read-only in intent, so it isn't an example of 'idempotent but not safe'.

options.text: POST
options.explanation: POST is neither safe nor idempotent. Sending the same POST twice can create two resources or run a process twice.

options.text: DELETE
options.explanation: Correct. DELETE changes server state (so it isn't safe), but deleting the same resource twice leaves the server in the same state as deleting it once (so it is idempotent). The second response may be 404, but idempotency is about server state, not identical responses.

options.text: HEAD
options.explanation: HEAD is a GET without the body, so it is safe and idempotent, just like GET.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Safe** = the client isn't asking for any state change. Among the core methods defined in RFC9110, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are safe; extensions can define other safe methods.
2. **Idempotent** = any number of identical requests leave the server in the same state as one. All safe methods, plus PUT and DELETE.
3. So 'idempotent but not safe' = {PUT, DELETE} minus the safe ones = PUT and DELETE.
4. Of the options, only DELETE is in that set.

Common trap: thinking DELETE isn't idempotent because the second call returns 404. Idempotency is defined by the effect on the server, not the response code.

questions.prompt: A payment POST charges the card but its response is lost. The client permits automatic timeout retries only for methods known to be idempotent, and this endpoint has no idempotency contract. What follows?

options.text: The library retries and the customer is charged twice
options.explanation: A blind retry could charge twice if the handler executes again. This client explicitly excludes automatic retries for such operations; HTTP itself does not implement payment deduplication.

options.text: The server detects the duplicate automatically because HTTP is stateless
options.explanation: REST statelessness does not prohibit stored resource state or deduplication records. HTTP simply does not infer payment deduplication from statelessness. Deduplication needs explicit state, such as a stored idempotency key.

options.text: TCP guarantees exactly-once delivery, so the retry can't happen
options.explanation: TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery within one connection. It says nothing about application-level retries over a *new* connection after a timeout, which is exactly this scenario.

options.text: The stated retry policy does not replay this POST automatically; the client has an ambiguous result and needs reconciliation or an idempotency contract
options.explanation: Correct. Automatic retries are normally limited to idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE...). For POST the client is left with an ambiguous timeout. The real fix is an idempotency key so that a retry is safe.

questions.workedExample:
1. The server charged the card, but the client did not receive confirmation.
2. From the client’s perspective, completion is unknown; in this scenario the charge actually happened.
3. The stated policy does not automatically retry an operation without known idempotent semantics.
4. RFC 9110 permits retrying a non-idempotent method when the client knows the operation is idempotent or knows the original was not applied; method name alone is not the entire rule.
5. A payment API needs a supported idempotency/reconciliation contract. Merely adding an arbitrary header does not create one.

questions.prompt: An API applies `PATCH /accounts/5` with an instruction to increment the balance. A proxy delivers that same request more than once. What does this reveal?

options.text: Each delivery can apply another increment; this operation is not idempotent.
options.explanation: Correct. Repeating a delta changes the intended effect again unless a separate deduplication contract protects it.

options.text: PATCH is always idempotent.
options.explanation: PATCH describes a partial change; whether repeating that change is idempotent depends on its semantics.

options.text: HTTP automatically discards duplicate PATCH requests.
options.explanation: HTTP does not supply an application deduplication record for this operation.

options.text: PATCH cannot change numeric fields.
options.explanation: Numeric changes are allowed; the issue is the meaning of repetition.

questions.workedExample: Compare an instruction to add money with one to set an absolute value. Repeating the addition compounds it. Repeating an absolute assignment can preserve the same intended result, although concurrency still needs its own protection. A method name alone does not turn an increment into an idempotent operation.

questions.prompt: PUT replaces writable user fields, adds an audit row and changes an informational updatedAt timestamp that does not trigger billing, notifications or application decisions. Does this incidental bookkeeping alone invalidate idempotency?

options.text: The reviewer: any change between two calls, including a timestamp, breaks idempotency
options.explanation: Idempotency in RFC 9110 is about the *intended effect* the client asked for, not every byte the server writes. Incidental side effects such as logs and bookkeeping timestamps don't count.

options.text: The reviewer: PUT is only idempotent when it returns 204
options.explanation: Idempotency doesn't depend on the response code or body. Two identical PUTs may return different responses and still be idempotent.

options.text: Neither: PUT is idempotent by definition, so the implementation can do anything
options.explanation: The method's semantics are a promise your implementation must keep. A PUT handler that appended a line item on every call would break that promise, and retries would then cause real harm.

options.text: The endpoint is still idempotent: the client's intended effect (user 7 has this representation) is the same after one call or five; audit rows and timestamps are incidental side effects
options.explanation: Correct. RFC 9110 explicitly allows idempotent and even safe methods to have side effects such as logging. What matters is that repeating the request doesn't change the outcome the client asked for.

questions.workedExample:
RFC 9110 defines a method as idempotent if the *intended effect on the server* of several identical requests is the same as one.

1. Intended effect of `PUT /users/7`: 'user 7 now looks like this body'.
2. After 1 call: user 7 matches the body. After 5 calls: still matches. ✔
3. Audit log has 5 rows instead of 1, and `updatedAt` moved. The client didn't ask for those, and repeating them causes no harm.

Contrast with a handler that, say, sends a 'profile updated' SMS on every PUT. That's a side effect users *notice*, so retries would be visible and you'd want to deduplicate.

lessons.title: Status codes and retry decisions
lessons.summary: Use response status codes to describe completion, validation and transient failure.
lessons.body:
HTTP status codes are part of the API contract. The method semantics from the preceding unit still apply when a response suggests trying again.

## Status codes

Status codes are the first thing a client, a load balancer and your monitoring look at. Use them precisely.

| Range | Meaning | Who should act |
|---|---|---|
| 2xx | Success | Interpret completion and content |
| 3xx | Redirect / not modified | Follow redirect or reuse validated content |
| 4xx | Client-error class | Interpret the specific code; some conditions are transient |
| 5xx | Server error | Server; client may retry |

The ones you'll use most:

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| 200 OK | Successful request; content depends on method (HEAD has no response content) |
| 201 Created | A request created a resource (e.g. POST or PUT); usually identify it with `Location` |
| 202 Accepted | Accepted for processing, not yet completed; completion is not guaranteed |
| 204 No Content | Success, empty body |
| 304 Not Modified | Conditional GET/HEAD validator indicates the selected representation need not be transferred |
| 400 Bad Request | Malformed syntax or invalid input |
| 401 Unauthorized | Missing or bad credentials |
| 403 Forbidden | Understood, but refused |
| 404 Not Found | No such resource |
| 409 Conflict | Clashes with current state |
| 412 Precondition Failed | `If-Match` ETag didn't match |
| 422 Unprocessable Content | Well-formed but semantically invalid |
| 429 Too Many Requests | Rate limited |
| 500 Internal Server Error | Unexpected server condition prevented fulfillment |
| 502 / 504 | Upstream failed / timed out |
| 503 Service Unavailable | Overloaded or in maintenance |

The 4xx/5xx split is a contract about retries. Most 4xx responses require correcting the request, but codes such as 408 and 429 can describe transient conditions. A 5xx may also be transient; the specific status, retry guidance and operation semantics determine whether retrying is appropriate. Returning `500` for a validation error makes clients retry pointlessly; returning `400` for a database outage makes them give up when they shouldn't.

"Might work later" still only licenses an automatic retry if the request is idempotent (or the endpoint enforces an applicable idempotency contract). A `500` on a `POST /payments` doesn't tell you whether the charge happened before the crash.

## Key takeaways
- Use 201 for creation and 202 for work accepted but not completed.
- Validation failures and dependency outages need different status codes.
- Retry guidance is only useful alongside the operation’s idempotency contract.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
- [MDN: HTTP response status codes](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status)

questions.prompt: During a database outage, your API catches the exception and returns `400 Bad Request` with `{"error": "could not save"}`. What is the main operational problem with this choice?

options.text: 400 responses can't have a JSON body
options.explanation: A 400 response can carry JSON error details. Some statuses, including 204 and 304, cannot carry response content, so this is not true of every status.

options.text: Load balancers will mark the server unhealthy on any 400
options.explanation: Load balancer health checks typically hit a dedicated endpoint, and passive checks look for 5xx or connection failures. Whether 400 affects health depends on configured active/passive checks; it is not a universal load-balancer rule.

options.text: 400 is reserved for CORS errors
options.explanation: 400 is a general 'bad request' code for malformed or invalid input. It has nothing specifically to do with CORS.

options.text: Clients may interpret 400 as a request error, and monitors counting only 5xx can miss the server outage
options.explanation: Correct. The 4xx/5xx split is a contract. A 400 tells clients the request itself is at fault, so they won't retry, and it hides a server-side outage from error-rate monitors that track 5xx. The right code is 503 (perhaps with Retry-After) or 500.

questions.workedExample:
Think about who reads status codes and what they do:

| Reader | Sees 400 | Sees 503 |
|---|---|---|
| Client retry logic | Give up | Back off, retry |
| SLO dashboard | Client error | Server error |
| Pager alerting | Silent | Fires |

These are risks for the illustrated monitoring/retry policies, not automatic behavior of all clients or monitors. Retries also require safe operation semantics. Use 503 (with `Retry-After` if you know roughly when you'll recover) or 500.

questions.prompt: Your generic HTTP client wrapper retries automatically with exponential backoff. For which of these responses is an **automatic** retry of the same request reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.text: `GET /orders/42` returned `503` with `Retry-After: 5`
options.explanation: Correct. 503 is a temporary server-side condition, GET is idempotent, and the server even told you how long to wait.

options.text: `POST /orders` (no idempotency key) returned `500`
options.explanation: Not safe to retry automatically. A 500 doesn't say whether the order was created before the crash, and POST isn't idempotent, so a retry could create a duplicate.

options.text: `PUT /users/7` returned `422`
options.explanation: No. 422 says the body itself is semantically invalid. Sending the identical body again will get the identical answer.

options.text: `GET /search?q=van` returned `429` with `Retry-After: 30`
options.explanation: Correct, as long as you honour the wait. 429 means 'you are over your limit for now'; retrying after the indicated delay is exactly what the server is asking for.

options.text: `DELETE /sessions/9` timed out with no response
options.explanation: Correct. DELETE is idempotent, so even if the first attempt succeeded, repeating it leaves the server in the same state.

questions.workedExample:
An automatic retry needs **both** of these to be true:

1. The failure is plausibly *transient* (5xx, 429, timeout, connection reset), not a 4xx that will repeat.
2. Repeating the request is *harmless*: the method is idempotent, or the endpoint enforces an applicable idempotency-key contract.

| Case | Transient? | Harmless? | Retry |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET 503 | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| POST 500 | Yes | No | No |
| PUT 422 | No | Yes | No |
| GET 429 | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| DELETE timeout | Yes | Yes | Yes |

The POST case is the classic trap: the status code says 'maybe later', but the method says 'not safe to repeat'.

questions.prompt: `POST /reports` kicks off a PDF export that takes about two minutes. What's the most RESTful response?

options.text: Hold the connection open for two minutes, then return `200` with the PDF
options.explanation: A long-lived request can exceed client, proxy or load-balancer timeouts and ties completion to that connection. A 202 with a status resource separates acceptance from eventual completion.

options.text: `201 Created` with the finished PDF in the body
options.explanation: The specified option incorrectly promises a finished PDF before it exists. An API could legitimately return 201 for a newly created job resource, but 202 is a natural choice when the requested processing remains incomplete.

options.text: `204 No Content`, and the client polls `/reports` until a new one appears
options.explanation: The specified response gives no job identifier; although 204 may include headers, polling the whole collection is a poor way to identify this job. Polling a whole collection to find 'the new one' is fragile.

options.text: `202 Accepted` with a `Location` header pointing at a status resource such as `/reports/jobs/81`, which the client polls (or is notified about by webhook)
options.explanation: Correct. 202 means 'accepted for processing, not finished'. Giving the job its own URL turns the long operation into an ordinary resource the client can GET.

questions.workedExample:
1. The work outlives a sensible request timeout, so don't do it inline.
2. Respond immediately with **202 Accepted** and a link to a job resource:

```
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Location: /reports/jobs/81
```

3. The client polls `GET /reports/jobs/81`, which reports `queued`, then `running`, then `done` with a link to `/reports/81.pdf`.
4. For many clients or long jobs, add a webhook so they don't have to poll.

The pattern makes a slow process look like a resource, which is the REST way to model it.

lessons.title: Authentication, conflict and quota errors
lessons.summary: Distinguish 401 from 403, 409 from 422, and client quotas from temporary unavailability.
lessons.body:
Clients recover differently from expired credentials, insufficient permissions, conflicting state and rate limits. Choosing the right code lets them respond to the actual condition.

## Pairs people mix up

**401 vs 403.** Despite its name, `401 Unauthorized` means *unauthenticated*: the credentials are missing, expired or invalid. RFC 9110 requires a 401 to carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header telling the client how to authenticate, and the client's natural reaction is to refresh its token and try again. `403 Forbidden` means the server understood the request and refuses it. Repeating unchanged credentials should not be an automatic recovery strategy, although different credentials or changed permissions can sometimes resolve it. A valid token without the right role or scope gets a 403.

**409 vs 422.** `409 Conflict` means the request clashes with the *current state of the resource*: a username that's already taken, or cancelling an order that has already shipped. The same request might succeed once the state changes. `422 Unprocessable Content` means the body is syntactically fine but *semantically* invalid on its own: an end date before the start date, or a negative quantity. Many APIs use plain `400` for validation failures; that's acceptable as long as you're consistent.

**429 and 503.** Both mean "not now", and both should ideally carry a `Retry-After` header (seconds, or an HTTP date). `429 Too Many Requests` is about *this client* exceeding its quota; `503` indicates temporary unavailability for this request; other endpoints or clients may still be served.

A well-formed create looks like this. Note the `201` and the `Location` header pointing at the new resource:

```
POST /orders HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"sku": "VAN-123", "qty": 1}
```

```
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /orders/9831
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": "9831", "status": "pending"}
```

## Key takeaways
- 401 requires a WWW-Authenticate challenge; unchanged credentials are not a general recovery strategy for 403.
- 409 describes conflict with current state; 422 describes well-formed content that cannot be processed semantically.
- 429 identifies a client limit; 503 identifies temporary unavailability for the request.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
- [MDN: HTTP response status codes](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status)

questions.prompt: A client sends `GET /invoices/77` with a valid token. The invoice exists but belongs to a different company, and the user's role isn't allowed to see it. Which status code is most appropriate?

options.text: 401 Unauthorized
options.explanation: Despite its name, 401 means *unauthenticated*: the server doesn't know who you are, or your credentials are missing or invalid. Here the token is valid, so identity is known.

options.text: 403 Forbidden
options.explanation: Correct. The server knows who the caller is (valid token) but the caller isn't permitted to access this resource. That's exactly what 403 means. (Some APIs return 404 instead to avoid revealing the invoice exists, which is a legitimate privacy choice.)

options.text: 400 Bad Request
options.explanation: 400 is for malformed or invalid requests. The request here is perfectly well-formed; the problem is permissions.

options.text: 500 Internal Server Error
options.explanation: 500 describes an unexpected server condition preventing fulfillment; it is not limited to programming bugs. A permission denial is an expected outcome, and a 5xx would wrongly encourage clients to retry and would page your on-call engineer.

questions.workedExample:
Ask two questions in order:

1. **Do we know who this is?** The token is valid, so yes. That rules out 401 (which is really 'unauthenticated').
2. **Are they allowed to do this?** No, the invoice belongs to another tenant.

'Known but not allowed' = **403**. If you don't want to leak the existence of other tenants' invoice IDs, returning **404** is also defensible, and many multi-tenant APIs (GitHub for private repos, for example) do exactly that.

questions.prompt: Your sign-up endpoint `POST /users` receives two bad requests. Request A has a valid body, but the email is already registered. Request B has `{"birthDate": "2031-01-01"}`, a date in the future. Which pair of status codes fits best?

options.explanation: This is the pair swapped. The duplicate email clashes with existing server state (409); the future birth date is invalid on its own terms, whatever the database holds (422).
Correct. A conflicts with the current state of the user collection: the same body would succeed if that email weren't taken. B is well-formed JSON that is semantically invalid regardless of state.
A unique-constraint violation is an expected outcome, not a server bug. Letting the database exception bubble up as a 500 makes clients retry and pages your on-call engineer for nothing.
403 means the server refuses fulfillment, often but not exclusively for authorisation reasons. Nothing here is about permissions; the caller is allowed to sign up, just not with that email.

questions.workedExample:
Ask one question of each failure: *would this request succeed if the server's state were different?*

- **A (duplicate email):** yes. If no user had that email, the same body would work. That's a clash with current state, so **409 Conflict**.
- **B (future birth date):** no. No state of the database makes a future birth date valid. That's a semantic validation error, so **422 Unprocessable Content** (or plain 400, if that's your API's convention).

The useful consequence for clients: a 409 suggests showing 'that email is taken' and perhaps offering a login link, while a 422 points at a field to fix.

questions.prompt: Your API returns `403 Forbidden` when an access token has **expired**. The mobile team reports that users get stuck on an error screen until they log out and back in, even though the app holds a valid refresh token. What's the best fix?

options.text: Return `401` with a `WWW-Authenticate` header for expired or invalid tokens, and keep `403` for valid tokens that lack permission
options.explanation: Correct. For this bearer-token API, an expired token maps to 401 with an authentication challenge. Reserve 403 for refusal despite the presented credentials; blindly refreshing the same permissions does not fix that refusal.

options.text: Return `400`, because an expired token is a malformed request
options.explanation: The request is well-formed. 400 is also treated as 'fix your request' by clients, so it doesn't trigger a token refresh either.

options.text: Keep `403` and make the client refresh its token on every 403
options.explanation: This would make clients refresh tokens pointlessly on every genuine permission denial, and it hides the difference between 'who are you?' and 'you can't do that' from every other consumer of the API.

options.text: Return `419 Authentication Timeout`
options.explanation: 419 isn't defined by RFC 9110; it's a framework-specific code (Laravel uses it for CSRF failures). Generic clients won't know what to do with it.

questions.workedExample:
Map each failure to what the client should *do next*:

| Situation | Next action | Code |
|---|---|---|
| No token | Log in | 401 |
| Expired token | Refresh, retry | 401 |
| Valid token, wrong role | Show 'no access' | 403 |

RFC 9110 also requires a 401 to include `WWW-Authenticate`, e.g. `Bearer error="invalid_token"` (the format OAuth's RFC 6750 defines). Configure the client to recognise the invalid_token challenge and make a bounded refresh attempt. HTTP does not make every library refresh automatically, and 403 does not prove different credentials could never help.

lessons.title: Stateless requests and HTTP validators
lessons.summary: Keep servers replaceable and use ETags for cache revalidation and atomic update checks.
lessons.body:
Interchangeable servers require requests that do not depend on one server’s private conversation history. HTTP validators then make reads and writes cheaper or safer.

## Statelessness

REST requires that **each request contains everything the server needs to understand it**. The server doesn't remember anything about the client between requests: no "current page" or "logged-in user" held in a particular server's memory.

```
       +---------+
req -->|   LB    |
       +---------+
       /    |    \
   +---+  +---+  +---+
   |A  |  |B  |  |C  |  any server
   +---+  +---+  +---+  can serve
       \    |    /      any request
      +-----------+
      | shared DB |
      +-----------+
```

This is what makes horizontal scaling easy. If server A dies, B and C carry on, because nothing the client depends on lived only in A. You don't need sticky sessions at the load balancer.

Statelessness doesn't mean the *application* has no state. Orders still live in the database. Strict REST keeps conversational session context in client requests. A shared server-side session store is a common practical HTTP API design that makes application servers replaceable, but it does not by itself satisfy Fielding's strict stateless-session constraint.

The cost is that each request is a little bigger and the server re-validates credentials every time. That's almost always worth paying.

## Caching and conditional requests

Because `GET` is safe and responses are self-describing, HTTP can cache them. The server controls this with headers:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=60
ETag: "v7-a1b2"
```

After 60 seconds a client retaining the response can revalidate; when the representation is unchanged:

```
GET /products/5
If-None-Match: "v7-a1b2"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
```

ETags also prevent **lost updates**. Two admins load product 5 at version `"v7"`. Both edit and `PUT` with `If-Match: "v7"`. The first succeeds and the version becomes `"v8"`. The second gets `412 Precondition Failed` instead of silently overwriting the first admin's change. This is optimistic concurrency control over HTTP, provided validator comparison and mutation are atomic.

## The other constraints, briefly

Fielding's full list also includes client–server separation, a layered system (clients can't tell if they're talking to a proxy), and HATEOAS (responses include links to the next possible actions). The Richardson Maturity Model grades APIs from level 0 (one endpoint, RPC over HTTP) to level 3 (hypermedia). A pragmatic API can use level 2: resources plus proper verbs and status codes. This is useful, although it does not satisfy all of Fielding's REST constraints.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Editing the same draft
> **How it maps:** Two editors start from revision 4. Accepting an edit only if revision 4 is still current prevents the second editor silently replacing a newer revision. If-Match applies the same check to a representation tag.
>
> **Where it stops:** An ETag is an opaque validator, not necessarily a numbered revision. The check and update must be atomic, and retries still need an application decision.

## Key takeaways
- Strict REST carries conversational context in requests; shared application state can still live in a database.
- If-None-Match revalidates a cached representation without resending unchanged content.
- If-Match prevents lost updates only when validator comparison and mutation are atomic.
- REST also includes separation, layering and hypermedia constraints.

## Further reading
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
- [Fielding's dissertation, chapter 5: REST](https://ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/rest_arch_style.htm)
- [Martin Fowler: Richardson Maturity Model](https://martinfowler.com/articles/richardsonMaturityModel.html)
- [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching)

questions.prompt: Assume interchangeable servers with access to the same required resource state and valid credentials. Which of these are consequences of a REST API being **stateless**? Select all that apply.

options.text: Any server behind the load balancer can handle any request, so sticky sessions aren't needed
options.explanation: Correct. Because no client context lives in one server's memory, requests can be routed anywhere, which makes scaling out and failover simple.

options.text: The API can't store any data in a database
options.explanation: Wrong. Statelessness is about *session* state between requests, not application data. Orders, users and so on live in the database as usual.

options.text: Authenticated requests carry the required authentication information rather than depending on a prior login remembered by one app instance
options.explanation: For authenticated operations, the request carries the authentication information needed to interpret it. A shared server-side session store makes instances replaceable but does not itself satisfy strict REST stateless-session constraints; public requests need no credentials.

options.text: If a server crashes mid-session, the client's next request can succeed on another server without re-login
options.explanation: Correct. Nothing the client depends on was held only in the crashed server's memory, so another instance can serve it.

options.text: Responses can never be cached
options.explanation: Wrong. Statelessness actually *helps* caching, because a response depends only on the request, not on hidden per-connection state. REST lists cacheability as a separate constraint that works alongside statelessness.

questions.workedExample:
Define the term precisely first: *stateless* means each request contains all the information needed to process it; the server keeps no client session context between requests.

Then test each option:

- Routing anywhere: follows directly. ✔
- No database: confuses session state with application state. ✘
- Auth per request: follows directly, since the server can't 'remember' you. ✔
- Survive a crash: follows directly. ✔
- No caching: the opposite is true. ✘

questions.prompt: Two support agents open product 5 (ETag `"v7"`). Agent A changes the price and sends `PUT /products/5` with `If-Match: "v7"`. One second later Agent B changes the description and sends `PUT /products/5` with `If-Match: "v7"`. What should happen to B's request in a correctly designed API?

options.text: 200 OK, and B's PUT overwrites the product, including A's new price
options.explanation: That's the 'lost update' problem that `If-Match` exists to prevent. Without the precondition check, B's full replacement would silently revert A's price change.

options.text: 409 Conflict, because two people edited at once
options.explanation: 409 is sometimes used for state conflicts, but HTTP defines a more specific code for a failed precondition header: 412. Using 412 tells the client exactly which mechanism rejected it.

options.text: 412 Precondition Failed, because the current ETag is now `"v8"`, not `"v7"`
options.explanation: Correct. A's successful write bumped the version to `"v8"`. B's `If-Match: "v7"` no longer matches, so the server refuses the write. B's client should re-fetch, merge and retry.

options.text: 304 Not Modified, because the ETag is unchanged
options.explanation: 304 is the response to a *conditional GET* with `If-None-Match` when the selected representation matches the validator; the cached response may have been stale before validation. It doesn't apply to a PUT, and the ETag *has* changed.

questions.workedExample:
This is optimistic concurrency control over HTTP.

```
t=0  A, B GET  -> ETag "v7"
t=1  A PUT If-Match "v7" -> match
     server writes, ETag -> "v8"
t=2  B PUT If-Match "v7"
     current is "v8" -> no match
     -> 412 Precondition Failed
```

B's client then:
1. `GET /products/5` (gets `"v8"` with A's price).
2. Re-applies B's description edit.
3. `PUT` with `If-Match: "v8"`. Succeeds.

No lock was held during user editing; the server must check the validator atomically with mutation, which may use a database lock. Neither edit was silently overwritten.

lessons.title: API styles and fetching trade-offs
lessons.summary: Compare resource, graph and RPC contracts, then diagnose over-fetching and under-fetching.
lessons.body:
"Should this be REST, GraphQL or gRPC?" comes up in nearly every design discussion. There's no universal winner. Each style optimises for a different consumer and a different set of pain points.

## The three styles at a glance

| | REST | GraphQL | gRPC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model | Resources | Typed graph | Procedures |
| Common transport | HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 | Usually HTTP; subscriptions use a chosen transport | Native gRPC commonly HTTP/2 |
| Payload | JSON (usually) | JSON | Protobuf binary |
| Contract | OpenAPI (optional) | GraphQL schema (required) | `.proto` (required) |
| HTTP caching | Native HTTP cache rules | Requires careful query/cache design | No ordinary response-cache contract |
| Browser support | Native HTTP | Native HTTP | Needs compatible protocol |
| Streaming | HTTP streams such as SSE | GraphQL subscriptions | 4 modes, native |

## REST: simple, cacheable, but chatty

REST's strengths are covered in the earlier REST units: universal tooling, CDN caching, easy debugging with `curl`. Its weaknesses show up when one screen needs data from many resources.

Imagine a mobile feed showing 20 posts, each with its author's name and avatar and the first 3 comments.

```
GET /feed              -> 20 post ids
GET /posts/1 ... /20   -> 20 calls
GET /users/a ... /t    -> up to 20
GET /posts/1/comments  -> 20 more
```

Counting them shows where the number comes from:

One list request plus up to three requests per post means up to 61 requests for this screen. Repeated authors or compound endpoints can reduce that fan-out.

That's up to 61 requests, not necessarily 61 sequential round trips. On an illustrative mobile link with 100 ms RTT, even with HTTP/2 multiplexing it's several dependent waves. And each response contains fields the screen doesn't need.

- **Under-fetching**: one call doesn't return enough, so you make more.
- **Over-fetching**: each call returns more than you need, wasting bandwidth and battery.

The usual REST fixes are compound endpoints (`GET /feed?include=author,comments`) or sparse fieldsets (`?fields=id,title`). They work, but every new screen tends to grow a new bespoke endpoint.

## Key takeaways
- Choose a style around its consumers, transport and contract.
- Under-fetching adds calls; over-fetching sends unused fields.
- Compound endpoints and sparse fieldsets reduce REST chatter; request count is not sequential round-trip count.

## Further reading
- [GraphQL: Introduction to GraphQL](https://graphql.org/learn/)
- [gRPC: Core concepts](https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/)

questions.prompt: A mobile screen needs a user's name and avatar, but `GET /users/7` returns 40 fields including address history and preferences. What is this problem called?

options.text: Under-fetching
options.explanation: Under-fetching is when one call *doesn't* return enough, forcing extra round trips. Here the call returns too much.

options.text: The N+1 problem
options.explanation: N+1 is about issuing one query for a list plus one per item. This scenario is a single request that returns unnecessary fields.

options.text: Head-of-line blocking
options.explanation: Head-of-line blocking is a transport issue where one slow packet or request delays those behind it. It's unrelated to response size.

options.text: Over-fetching
options.explanation: Correct. The client receives far more data than it needs, wasting bandwidth, parse time and battery. GraphQL field selection or REST sparse fieldsets (`?fields=name,avatarUrl`) address it.

questions.workedExample:
Classify by the *direction* of the mismatch:

- Response has **more** than needed → over-fetching.
- Response has **less** than needed, so more calls follow → under-fetching.

The screen needs 2 of 40 fields, so 38 are wasted. That's over-fetching. Fixes: `GET /users/7?fields=name,avatarUrl`, or a GraphQL query `{ user(id: 7) { name avatarUrl } }`.

lessons.title: GraphQL resolvers, batching and query costs
lessons.summary: Use DataLoader batching while controlling nested-query work and HTTP caching.
lessons.body:
One client request can still trigger many database queries. Follow the work inside the resolver tree, as well as the shape of the HTTP response.

## GraphQL: the client asks for exactly what it needs

GraphQL, open-sourced by Facebook in 2015, exposes a GraphQL schema. Clients send a query that mirrors the shape of the data they want, usually as `POST /graphql`.

```
query {
  feed(first: 20) {
    id
    title
    author { name avatarUrl }
    comments(first: 3) { text }
  }
}
```

One HTTP request selects the requested fields. Successful data follows that selection; errors and nullability can alter what is returned. The GraphQL schema supports introspection, so tools like GraphiQL give autocomplete and type-checking for free.

## The N+1 problem

GraphQL moves the fan-out from the client to the server. Each field is backed by a *GraphQL resolver* function. Naïve resolvers make the problem worse, not better:

```
feed resolver:   1 query  -> 20 posts
author resolver: called 20 times
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?
                 -> 20 queries
Total: 21 queries for these 20 posts
```

Follow how the work grows as the list gets longer:

With naïve per-item resolvers, every extra parent adds more database queries for its nested fields.

So adding comments takes it from 21 to 41 queries. Nest one more level and it multiplies, because each of those children has its own children.

The standard fix is **batching with a DataLoader**. Within one tick of the event loop, the loader collects every `author` id requested, then issues a single query:

```sql
-- Illustrative ids; bind real parameters.
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE id IN (a, b, c, ..., t)
```

When each nested field fits into one supported database batch:

Batching groups compatible loads across parents: one query for the list, one for authors and one for comments in this example.

So the example drops from 41 queries to 3. Parameter limits, batch-size caps and per-parent pagination can require additional work as the parent list grows. DataLoader also caches per request, so the same author appearing on five posts is fetched once.

> [!warning] GraphQL's operational costs
> - **Caching**: if operations use `POST /graphql`, ordinary URL-based CDN caching cannot distinguish request bodies. GraphQL queries may also use GET; mutation operations must not execute through GET. Teams use *persisted queries* (send a hash; allow `GET`) to recover some of this.
> - **Abuse**: a client can write a deeply nested query that fans out to millions of rows. You need query depth limits, complexity scoring and timeouts. GitHub's GraphQL API, for example, charges each query "points" from the connections and backing requests needed.
> - **Errors**: many deployed GraphQL APIs return `200 OK` with an `errors` array. Status handling depends on the transport contract and response media type; inspect GraphQL errors as well as HTTP status.

For a static potential-node budget, count each nesting level by multiplying the number of parents by the requested children per parent, then add the counts across levels. Pagination bounds each branch before any resolver runs; actual database work also depends on resolver implementation.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: One shopping list
> **How it maps:** Collecting everyone’s requests before visiting a shop avoids a separate trip for each person. DataLoader similarly groups compatible loads into a batch.
>
> **Where it stops:** A larger list still costs work. Batch size, data ordering, authorisation and per-parent pagination can require more than one backend request.

## Key takeaways
- GraphQL gives clients a typed response shape and moves fan-out to resolvers.
- Request-scoped DataLoader batches supported loads and caches repeated identities.
- Persisted read queries over GET can support ordinary URL caching; mutations must not execute through GET.
- Budget depth, potential node count and execution time; inspect GraphQL errors as well as HTTP status.

## Further reading
- [GraphQL: Introduction to GraphQL](https://graphql.org/learn/)
- [GraphQL: Performance (N+1 and DataLoader)](https://graphql.org/learn/performance/)
- [DataLoader on GitHub](https://github.com/graphql/dataloader)
- [GitHub: GraphQL query limits](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/overview/rate-limits-and-query-limits-for-the-graphql-api)

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query fetches posts with authors and tags. Naïve resolvers issue one database query per post for each nested field. All author loads fit one supported batch and all tag loads fit another. What changes with request-scoped batching?

options.text: Compatible loads are grouped, so adding posts need not add a database query for every author and tag.
options.explanation: Correct under the stated batch assumptions. The list query and supported field batches replace per-parent calls.

options.text: Only the top-level list can be batched.
options.explanation: DataLoader groups compatible nested loads too.

options.text: Nothing: GraphQL already batches database access automatically.
options.explanation: The GraphQL schema and query language do not implement backend batching for you.

options.text: Batching removes the need for authorisation and pagination.
options.explanation: Batching changes how data is loaded, not who may read it or how much may be requested.

questions.workedExample: Trace the backend calls, not just the HTTP request. Without batching, each parent triggers separate lookups. With supported batches, the resolver collects identities and asks for them together. Batch-size caps, parameter limits and nested pagination can still split the work.

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine drawbacks of exposing a **public** GraphQL API compared with REST? Select all that apply.

options.text: Responses can't easily be cached by CDNs because most queries go to `POST /graphql`
options.explanation: Correct for ordinary URL-based caching of POST queries: request bodies are not normally part of the cache key. Explicit POST caching can be defined, and persisted read queries over GET make ordinary URL caching practical.

options.text: Clients can craft deeply nested or wide queries that are very expensive, so you need depth limits and cost analysis
options.explanation: Correct. In REST the server decides each endpoint's cost. In GraphQL the client composes the query, so the server must defend itself. GitHub's API uses a points-based cost model for this reason.

options.text: GraphQL can't return nested data
options.explanation: Wrong. Returning nested data in one round trip is GraphQL's main selling point.

options.text: Errors often come back as `200 OK` with an `errors` array, which breaks tooling that relies on HTTP status codes
options.explanation: Correct for APIs using this common response convention. Inspect the errors field; transport status rules vary with the implementation and response media type, including evolving GraphQL-over-HTTP specifications.

options.text: GraphQL has no GraphQL schema, so clients can't discover fields
options.explanation: Wrong. GraphQL *requires* a GraphQL schema and supports introspection; discoverability is one of its strengths.

questions.workedExample: A public GraphQL API must control the client-selected work and choose a cache strategy. Ordinary URL caching does not distinguish POST bodies; persisted read queries over GET can help. Nested data and a typed schema are capabilities, not drawbacks. Under the common 200-with-errors convention, status-only monitoring misses GraphQL errors; check the deployed response contract and inspect the body too.

questions.prompt: A mobile app uses 40 known read-only GraphQL query shapes returning public, non-personalized cacheable data. It currently sends POST requests and the CDN does not cache them. Which approach enables ordinary URL-based caching?

options.text: Switch the CDN to cache POST responses by request body
options.explanation: CDNs generally don't cache POST, and keying on large, variably formatted bodies is fragile. It also does nothing to stop arbitrary queries hitting your origin.

options.text: Persisted queries: register the 40 queries ahead of time, have clients send `GET /graphql?id=<hash>&variables=...`, and let the CDN cache by URL
options.explanation: Correct for the stated public cacheable data. The registered query identity and variables form a URL cache key. An allow-list excludes unregistered shapes, but allowed variable values still need limits and all access rules still apply.

options.text: Add DataLoader to the resolvers
options.explanation: DataLoader batches and caches database lookups *within one request* on the server. It reduces N+1 queries but doesn't make responses cacheable at the CDN.

options.text: Return `Cache-Control: max-age=60` on the POST responses
options.explanation: Explicit POST caching is permitted by HTTP, but max-age alone does not make this CDN distinguish and cache different query bodies. The stated ordinary URL cache is best served by persisted read queries over GET.

questions.workedExample: Register known read-only query shapes, then send their identifiers and variables in GET URLs. Configure response cache headers and a cache key that distinguishes those variables. The stated data is public and non-personalised; private responses require a different cache policy. An allow-list reduces query-shape freedom but does not itself bound page sizes, authorise access or make an allowed query cheap.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL API budgets potential result size before execution. A query asks for many users, many followers per user and many repositories per follower. Why can the API reject it even before learning how many records actually exist?

options.text: Only the number of fields written in the query matters.
options.explanation: A short query can expand across large nested lists.

options.text: Nested list bounds multiply across levels, giving a potential expansion the API can reject.
options.explanation: Correct. Static bounds can expose excessive potential work even when actual data might be smaller.

options.text: Every query with more than one nesting level must fail.
options.explanation: Nesting can be legitimate; the configured budget and bounds matter.

options.text: The API cannot assess any cost until all resolvers finish.
options.explanation: Potential bounds, depth and complexity can be checked before execution.

questions.workedExample: A requested child limit applies separately to every parent. Another nested list multiplies that potential again. Add the work across levels when the chosen policy counts nodes. Rejecting an excessive upper bound protects the service before execution; actual database cost still depends on resolver behaviour.

lessons.title: Protobuf tags, varints and wire size
lessons.summary: Explain how field tags and varints affect message size, without assuming a universal compression or speed advantage.

questions.prompt: A protobuf field is `int32 qty = 2;`. Positive varints store seven value bits per byte. The value grows from 127 to 128 while the protobuf schema stays the same. Why can the encoded field grow?

options.text: Protobuf starts sending the field name.
options.explanation: Binary protobuf identifies fields by tag and wire type, not their names.

options.text: The field tag changes when the value changes.
options.explanation: The protobuf schema still assigns tag 2.

options.text: The value crosses the one-byte varint boundary and needs another value byte.
options.explanation: Correct. The tag stays fixed; the value representation grows.

options.text: Every int32 always occupies four value bytes.
options.explanation: Varint encoding is variable length, unlike a fixed-width integer encoding.

questions.workedExample: The field key identifies the same field in both messages. What changes is the integer payload: seven bits can represent values only through 127. The next value needs another varint byte. This is why small positive integers are compact, without implying that every integer uses the same space.

lessons.title: Evolving protobuf schemas safely
lessons.summary: Preserve field meaning across old and new binary readers by reserving removed tags.
lessons.body:
The previous unit showed that binary protobuf identifies fields by tags and wire types. Protobuf schema changes must preserve what deployed readers think each tag means. Wire compatibility also differs from source-code or business compatibility.

## Protobuf schema evolution rules

Because tags identify fields, you can evolve a protobuf schema safely if you:

- **Add** new fields with **new** tag numbers. Old readers ignore unknown tags.
- **Never reuse** a removed field's tag. Mark it `reserved 3;`.
- **Do not change** a field's tag number. Prefer a new field rather than changing its type; the proto3 guide permits some wire-compatible type changes, but their value ranges and application semantics still need review.

Break these rules and you get silent damage, not an error. If you reuse tag 3 for a new field with the same *wire type* (say, one `string` replaced by another), an old client happily reads the new value as the old field. If the wire types differ, most parsers set the field aside as unknown, so the old client just sees it as missing.

Renaming a field is safe for the binary format, because names never go on the wire. It does break anything that uses protobuf's JSON mapping, which keys by field name.

For binary proto3 messages with implicit scalar presence, a deleted field can be treated as unknown by the other reader, and a missing scalar reads as its default. Reserve both the removed tag and its old name; this does not guarantee that an application which required the field will still behave correctly.

## Key takeaways
- Add fields with unused tags and reserve removed tags and names.
- Reusing a tag can silently reinterpret data; changing wire types can make an old reader treat it as unknown.
- Renaming a field preserves the binary encoding but can break JSON-mapping consumers.

## Further reading
- [Protocol Buffers: Language guide (proto3)](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/)

questions.prompt: A proto message has `string email = 3;`. You delete the field and later add `int64 loyalty_points = 3;`. Some old clients are still deployed. What happens when an old client reads a new message?

options.text: The old client gets a clear decoding error
options.explanation: Protobuf parsers are deliberately lenient. They may not raise an error, which is why this is dangerous: the corruption can be silent.

options.text: Nothing; protobuf matches fields by name
options.explanation: Protobuf matches by **tag number**, not by name. Names aren't on the wire at all, so renaming is safe but reusing a tag is not.

options.text: A conforming reader sees a wire-type mismatch and normally treats the new value as an unknown field, leaving email unset; reusing tags is still forbidden
options.explanation: Correct. The field number matches but wire type 0 does not match the old string field’s type 2. Typical generated parsers preserve or skip it as unknown. Reusing the same number with a compatible wire type can instead silently assign the wrong meaning. Reserve removed numbers.

options.text: Old clients automatically download the new protobuf schema
options.explanation: Protobuf has no runtime protobuf schema exchange. Clients use whatever generated code they were compiled with.

questions.workedExample: The old protobuf schema expects tag 3 with the length-delimited wire type used for a string. The new message uses the varint wire type for int64. A conforming reader normally treats that incompatible field as unknown, leaving email unset. Reusing a tag remains forbidden: a different same-wire-type replacement could silently reinterpret data. Reserve deleted field numbers and names.

questions.prompt: Old and new services exchange binary proto3 messages using implicit scalar presence. Considering wire compatibility only (not source API or business-required fields), which changes are safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Add `string nickname = 9;` (tag 9 never used before)
options.explanation: Safe. Old readers skip the unknown tag 9; new readers see the default (empty string) when old writers omit it.

options.text: Rename `string sku = 1;` to `string product_code = 1;`
options.explanation: Safe for binary protobuf, because only the tag goes on the wire. (It would break JSON-mapped traffic, which uses names, but that isn't in play here.)

options.text: Change `int32 qty = 2;` to `string qty = 2;`
options.explanation: Unsafe. Changing type on the same tag changes the wire type, so old readers will drop or misparse the field. Add a new field with a new tag instead.

options.text: Delete `string email = 3;` and add `reserved 3; reserved "email";`
options.explanation: Safe. Old readers just see `email` as missing (empty), and `reserved` stops anyone accidentally reusing the tag or name later.

options.text: Delete `email = 3` and reuse tag 3 for `string phone = 3;`
options.explanation: Unsafe, and the worst kind. Same wire type, so old readers will silently show phone numbers as email addresses.

questions.workedExample: Binary protobuf identifies a field by number and wire type. A fresh unused number can be ignored by old readers. Renaming a field preserves binary identity but can break generated source or JSON clients. Reserve deleted numbers and names; do not reuse them. Changing int32 to string changes the wire type and is not the safe migration described here.

lessons.title: gRPC streaming, deadlines and API selection
lessons.summary: Choose streaming modes, propagate deadlines and account for browser and load-balancing constraints.
lessons.body:
A compact message format is only part of a service contract. Consumers also need suitable streaming, cancellation, browser access and routing.

## Four streaming modes

gRPC runs on HTTP/2, which multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection. That enables:

| Mode | Example |
|---|---|
| Unary | `GetStock` request/response |
| Server streaming | Live price feed |
| Client streaming | Upload telemetry batch |
| Bidirectional | Chat, collaborative edit |

gRPC supports **deadline propagation**. Some language implementations do it automatically; others require enabling it or passing the incoming context/deadline to outgoing calls. With propagation configured, a 300 ms caller budget can shrink at each downstream hop.

## gRPC's downsides

- **Browsers** can't speak raw gRPC (they can't control HTTP/2 framing or read trailers). You need gRPC-Web, usually translated by a proxy such as Envoy, or a browser-friendly variant such as Connect.
- **Debugging** binary payloads needs tooling (`grpcurl`), not just `curl`.
- **Load balancing** is trickier. Long-lived HTTP/2 connections mean an L4 load balancer pins all of a client's calls to one backend. You need L7 (request-level) balancing or client-side balancing. The networking module covers this.

## Choosing

```
Who calls the API?
 |
 +- Public / third-party devs
 |    -> REST (+ OpenAPI)
 |
 +- Your own UIs, many screens,
 |  varied data needs
 |    -> GraphQL (or a BFF)
 |
 +- Internal microservices,
    latency-sensitive, polyglot
      -> gRPC
```

Real systems usually mix them. A common pattern:

```
 Mobile/Web         Partners
     |                  |
  GraphQL             REST
  gateway            public API
     \                 /
      +-- gRPC mesh --+
      | svc  svc  svc |
      +---------------+
```

These styles can coexist without requiring every consumer to use the same interface. The decision depends on the documented client contract and measured workload.

> [!tip] Interview framing
> Don't pick one and defend it to the death. Say who the consumers are, what their latency and payload constraints are, whether you need streaming or CDN caching, and pick accordingly. Mentioning N+1 and how DataLoader fixes it is a strong signal.

## Key takeaways
- gRPC supports unary, server, client and bidirectional streaming.
- Deadline propagation needs appropriate implementation configuration and carries a shrinking caller budget.
- Browsers need a compatible protocol, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections complicate L4 balancing.
- A system can combine GraphQL or BFFs for UIs, REST for partners and gRPC internally.

## Further reading
- [gRPC: Core concepts](https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/)
- [gRPC: Performance best practices](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/performance/)
- [gRPC: Deadlines](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/)
- [gRPC-Web: Supported streaming modes](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-web)

questions.prompt: You migrate internal service calls from REST/JSON to gRPC. Behind an L4 (TCP) load balancer with 10 backends, you notice one backend at 90% CPU and the others nearly idle. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: Protobuf is slower to parse than JSON
options.explanation: Parsing performance depends on workload and implementation. It would not by itself explain why an L4 balancer pins a high-volume connection to one backend.

options.text: gRPC multiplexes many calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, and an L4 balancer only balances connections, so all of a client's requests stick to one backend
options.explanation: Correct under the stated connection-level balancer. Each TCP connection is assigned to a backend; a long-lived gRPC connection can carry many calls to that backend. HTTP/1.1 also supports persistent pooled connections, so it does not guarantee an even distribution. L7 or client-side balancing can distribute calls.

options.text: gRPC deadlines are concentrating retries on one server
options.explanation: Deadlines cause calls to fail fast when time runs out. They don't steer traffic to a particular backend.

options.text: The backend is running a different protobuf version
options.explanation: A version mismatch could cause decoding issues, but it wouldn't attract a disproportionate share of traffic to one host.

questions.workedExample:
1. L4 balancing decides at **TCP connect** time.
2. With HTTP/1.1, clients typically open a pool of connections and recycle them, so load spreads.
3. gRPC/HTTP/2 multiplexes: one connection carries hundreds of concurrent streams and lives for hours.
4. If a few large callers each hold one connection, those connections land on one or two backends, and stay there.

Fixes:
- L7 proxy (Envoy, Linkerd, gRPC-aware cloud LBs) that balances per **request**.
- Client-side load balancing: the client resolves all backend addresses and round-robins calls.
- Set a max connection age so connections are periodically re-established.

questions.prompt: A checkout service calls Pricing (which calls Tax, which calls a Currency service). The user-facing SLA is 500 ms. Pricing sometimes hangs for 5 s, and Tax keeps working on requests long after the user has given up. Which gRPC feature most directly addresses this wasted work?

options.text: Bidirectional streaming
options.explanation: Streaming changes the shape of the conversation (many messages each way), not whether downstream services know the caller has stopped waiting.

options.text: Server reflection
options.explanation: Reflection lets tools like `grpcurl` discover services at runtime. It has nothing to do with timeouts.

options.text: Deadline propagation: Checkout sets a 500 ms deadline that flows to Pricing, Tax and Currency, each of which can cancel when the remaining time hits zero
options.explanation: Correct when deadline propagation is configured. Downstream handlers can observe cancellation, but must cooperate by stopping their own work and canceling supported database/child operations; gRPC does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary application code.

options.text: Protobuf field tags
options.explanation: Field tags are about wire encoding and protobuf schema evolution, not about time budgets.

questions.workedExample: Set a deadline at the request boundary and propagate the remaining time downstream. A slow Pricing call then cannot silently give Tax and Currency a fresh full budget. RPC cancellation must reach application work too: handlers should stop tasks and release resources when cancelled. Deadline propagation bounds useful work; it does not guarantee the service will succeed.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing team explicitly wants (a) resource-oriented HTTP endpoints callable with ordinary tools for partners, (b) UI-specific response composition, and (c) generated protobuf RPC stubs and streaming internally. Which combination most directly fits these chosen constraints?

options.text: gRPC for all three, for consistency
options.explanation: gRPC is poor for (a): partners would need protobuf tooling and couldn't use plain HTTP clients. It's also awkward for the mobile web parts of (b) without gRPC-Web proxies.

options.text: (a) REST, (b) GraphQL or a BFF, (c) gRPC
options.explanation: Correct. Partners want something any language can call with documented, cacheable endpoints (REST + OpenAPI). The app benefits from fetching exactly the shape each screen needs (GraphQL or a BFF). High-volume internal calls benefit from protobuf's small payloads, generated stubs, deadlines and HTTP/2 multiplexing (gRPC).

options.text: (a) GraphQL, (b) REST, (c) REST
options.explanation: Public GraphQL and internal REST are valid designs, but this option does not provide the explicitly requested internal protobuf RPC stubs and gRPC streaming contract. No universal CPU or latency comparison follows from a request rate alone.

options.text: REST for all three, because it's the most widely understood
options.explanation: REST can use compound responses, streaming HTTP and application deadlines. This option still does not meet the chosen requirement for generated protobuf RPC stubs and gRPC streaming internally.

questions.workedExample:
Match each consumer to the style's strengths:

| Consumer | Needs | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| Partners | Easy, stable, any language | REST |
| Rider app | Few round trips, varied shapes | GraphQL/BFF |
| Internal | Low latency, typed, high QPS | gRPC |

The combination follows the stated interface requirements. Actual payload savings, CPU cost and latency need workload-specific measurement; the earlier 60% byte saving is not universal.

questions.prompt: Your internal `Inventory` service speaks gRPC. The web team now wants to call it directly from a React app in the browser. What do they need?

options.text: Nothing: modern browsers use HTTP/2, so they can call gRPC endpoints directly
options.explanation: Browsers do use HTTP/2, but JavaScript can't control HTTP/2 framing or read the trailers gRPC uses for its status, so raw gRPC isn't callable from page code.

options.text: Convert the service to GraphQL first
options.explanation: That's a much bigger change than needed. GraphQL might suit a UI-facing gateway, but it isn't required just to reach a gRPC service from a browser.

options.text: Open a WebSocket to each gRPC backend
options.explanation: WebSockets are a different protocol. gRPC servers don't accept WebSocket connections, and you'd lose generated stubs and gRPC semantics.

options.text: gRPC-Web (or a browser-compatible protocol such as Connect), typically with a proxy such as Envoy translating to native gRPC
options.explanation: Correct. gRPC-Web carries gRPC semantics in a form browsers can send and read, and a proxy translates it to normal gRPC for the backend. You keep generated, typed clients.

questions.workedExample:
1. gRPC depends on HTTP/2 details: framing, and **trailers** carrying `grpc-status`.
2. Browser `fetch` gives page code no control over framing and no reliable access to trailers.
3. gRPC-Web moves the status into the response body and works over HTTP/1.1 or 2.
4. A proxy (commonly Envoy) translates gRPC-Web to native gRPC:

```
Browser --gRPC-Web--> Envoy
Envoy --gRPC (HTTP/2)--> Inventory
```

The referenced grpc-web implementation supports unary calls and server streaming in grpcwebtext mode; client and bidirectional streaming are not currently supported.

lessons.title: Bounded lists and offset pagination
lessons.summary: Bound list responses and trace why deep offsets cost more and shift under writes.
lessons.body:
An API is a promise. Once a client depends on it, every quirk becomes load-bearing. Good API design is mostly about making the right promises up front, so you can change the implementation for years without breaking anyone.

This unit bounds list results and examines offset pagination. Later units develop cursor contracts, query validation and compatibility.

## Pagination

No list endpoint should return unbounded results. A customer with 2 million orders will eventually call `GET /orders` and take down your database. Always paginate, with a sensible default and a hard maximum (Stripe v1 list APIs: default 10, maximum 100).

## Offset pagination

```
GET /orders?limit=20&offset=40
```

```sql
-- Walk past 40 rows before returning 20.
SELECT * FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;
```

It's simple and lets users jump to "page 37". But it has two serious problems.

**1. It gets slower the deeper you go.** The database can't jump to row 40,000. It has to walk the index and discard the first 40,000 rows, then return 20:

```formula reference
E_off ≈ offset + limit
cost = O(offset + limit)
where
E_off: the number of index entries the database walks to serve one offset page
offset: how many rows the client asks to skip (the offset query parameter)
limit: how many rows the page returns (the limit query parameter)
entries: index entries, one per row in the index
cost: the work the database does for one page
O(...): Big O notation: how the cost grows as the quantities inside the brackets grow, ignoring constant factors
≈: approximately equal to
In words: in this indexed scan, a deep offset still walks past the preceding entries before returning the requested page.
```

This assumes the database walks an index in sort order. Without a suitable index it is worse: it may sort the whole table first.

**2. Results shift under concurrent writes.**

```
Page 1 (offset 0):  [A B C D E]
  -- new order Z inserted at top --
Page 2 (offset 5):  [E F G H I]
                     ^ E seen twice
```

A deletion causes the opposite: an item is skipped entirely.

## Key takeaways
- Every list needs a default and maximum page size.
- An indexed offset scan still walks and discards the earlier entries.
- Concurrent inserts duplicate previously seen rows; deletions can skip rows.

## Further reading
- [Use The Index, Luke: Paging through results (no offset)](https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)
- [Stripe API: Pagination](https://docs.stripe.com/api/pagination)

questions.prompt: Why should every list endpoint enforce a maximum page size, even for authenticated, trusted clients?

options.text: Because JSON can't represent more than 1,000 array elements
options.explanation: JSON has no array size limit. The concern is cost, not format.

options.text: Because HTTP/1.1 limits responses to 1 MB
options.explanation: HTTP has no such limit; responses can be gigabytes. Again, the issue is resource cost on your side.

options.text: To make offset pagination stable under concurrent inserts
options.explanation: A page size cap doesn't fix offset's instability. Items still shift between pages when rows are inserted or deleted; keyset pagination with stable sort keys avoids those shifts; a stable snapshot is another option.

options.text: Because one request for an unbounded result set (e.g. 2 million orders) can exhaust database, memory and network resources and hurt every other client
options.explanation: Correct. A bounded page keeps each request's cost predictable. Stripe, for example, defaults to 10 and caps at 100. Trusted clients still have bugs, and one runaway loop can take the database down.

questions.workedExample: The page-size limit bounds work per request, not trust in the caller. A trusted client can still make a bug or ask for too much data. Large results occupy database work, memory and network capacity, so one request can harm other clients. Enforce a server maximum even when a client supplies its own limit.

questions.prompt: A user is paging through a feed sorted newest-first using `?limit=10&offset=N`. After they load page 1 (items 1–10), 3 new items are inserted at the top. What do they see on page 2 (`offset=10`)?

options.text: Items 11–20, as expected
options.explanation: Offset is evaluated against the *current* data, not the data at the time page 1 loaded. The 3 inserts shift every item down by 3 positions.

options.text: Items 8–17: the last three items from page 1 are shown again
options.explanation: Correct. After 3 inserts, old item 8 is now at position 11. `OFFSET 10` skips positions 1–10 and returns positions 11–20, which are old items 8–17. Items 8, 9 and 10 appear twice.

options.text: Items 14–23: three items are skipped
options.explanation: Skipping happens when items are *deleted* above the cursor position, shifting items up. Inserts shift items down, causing duplicates instead.

options.text: An error, because the data changed
options.explanation: Offset pagination has no way to detect changes; it silently returns whatever is at that position now.

questions.workedExample: The offset counts positions in the current result, not identities in the result the user already saw. Three new rows now precede the old first row. Skipping ten positions therefore skips the new three and only seven old rows, so the second page begins at old item 8 and repeats items 8–10. A stable keyset boundary avoids this particular shift.
