lessons.title: Quota policy and client signals
lessons.summary: Explain why limits exist and signal client quotas with 429, Retry-After and remaining allowance.
lessons.body:
Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a period. It's one of the most common system design interview questions, and one of the most important pieces of real API infrastructure.

## Why rate limit?

- **Protect the service.** One buggy client in a tight loop shouldn't take down everyone else.
- **Fairness.** Share capacity between tenants, so a noisy neighbour can't starve the rest.
- **Cost control.** Expensive endpoints (search, AI inference, SMS sending) cost real money per call.
- **Security.** Slow down credential stuffing, scraping and enumeration attacks.
- **Commercial tiers.** Free plan 60 requests/min, paid plan 5,000.

Stripe runs several limiters in layers: a request-rate limiter per user, a concurrent-requests limiter, and load shedders that drop low-priority traffic when the whole fleet is under stress.

## Signalling limits to clients

When a client is over its limit, return **429 Too Many Requests** (defined in RFC 6585), and tell it when to come back:

```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 12
RateLimit-Policy: "min";q=100;w=60
RateLimit: "min";r=0;t=12
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"title": "Rate limit exceeded",
 "detail": "100 requests per minute"}
```

- `Retry-After` is a standard header: seconds to wait, or an HTTP date.
- `RateLimit-Policy` and `RateLimit` are being standardised by the IETF (still a draft in 2026). The policy says "quota `q` = 100 per window `w` = 60 s"; `RateLimit` says how much is left (`r`) and the effective time window in seconds (`t`), rather than a universal guarantee of a full reset. Earlier drafts used three separate `RateLimit-Limit`, `-Remaining` and `-Reset` headers, which some gateways still emit, and many APIs (GitHub, for example) use the older `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. Note that GitHub's `X-RateLimit-Reset` is a Unix timestamp, not a number of seconds, so always read the docs.
- Send the remaining-quota headers on **successful** responses too, so well-behaved clients can slow down *before* hitting the wall.

Don't use `503` for per-client limits. `503` describes temporary inability to serve this request, which clients and monitors may handle differently. Load shedding or maintenance can legitimately use `503` even if other endpoints or clients are still served.

## Key takeaways
- Limits protect capacity, fairness, cost and accounts; request and concurrency limits have different jobs.
- Return 429 for a client quota and use Retry-After to guide recovery.
- Expose remaining allowance on successes too; header formats and reset units depend on the contract.

## Further reading
- [Stripe blog: Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [MDN: 429 Too Many Requests](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429)
- [IETF draft: RateLimit header fields for HTTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers/)
- [GitHub: Rate limits for the REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api)

questions.prompt: A client exceeds its per-user quota. Which response best follows HTTP conventions?

options.text: `503 Service Unavailable` with no headers
options.explanation: 503 means the *service* is unhealthy or overloaded for requests the service cannot currently handle. It triggers outage alerts and generic retry behaviour, and it hides the fact that this particular client is the problem.

options.text: `403 Forbidden`
options.explanation: 403 means the server refuses fulfilment; it is not the specific HTTP quota signal. Different credentials or permissions may sometimes resolve a 403, so it does not universally mean permanent denial.

options.text: `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header
options.explanation: Correct. RFC 6585 defines 429 for excessive request rates. Retry-After can provide a whole-second delay or an HTTP date; clients should respect it within their overall retry budget.

options.text: `200 OK` with an empty body
options.explanation: Pretending to succeed hides the problem: the client thinks its request worked, and your monitoring sees no errors.

questions.workedExample:
The specific condition is that this caller has exceeded a request quota, so 429 communicates it directly. A 403 is refusal, not necessarily permanent denial; a 503 indicates temporary inability to serve and does not require the whole service to be down. Include useful retry guidance when available.

```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
```

Provider-specific quota fields can add detail, but their units and reset semantics must be documented.

lessons.title: Token buckets, bursts and refill waits
lessons.summary: Separate burst capacity from sustained rate, refill lazily and tell rejected clients when another token can be ready.
lessons.body:
## Token bucket

A common algorithm. Each client has a bucket that holds up to **capacity** tokens. Tokens are added at a fixed **refill rate**. Each request takes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

```
  refill r tokens/s
        |
        v
   +---------+
   | o o o o |  capacity C
   | o o o   |
   +----+----+
        |
   1 token per request
   empty -> 429
```

Two parameters, two meanings:

- **Refill rate** = long-run average throughput.
- **Capacity** = largest burst allowed.

You don't need a timer to add tokens. Store the token count and the time of the last top-up, and when a request arrives, add the tokens that would have dripped in since then:

```formula reference
b_new = min(C, b_old + r × Δt)
where
b_new: the number of tokens in the bucket after the top-up
b_old: the tokens stored at the last top-up
C: the capacity, the most tokens the bucket can hold
r: the refill rate, in tokens per second
Δt: delta t, the time since the last top-up, in seconds
min: the smaller of the two values, so the bucket never overflows its capacity
In words: add tokens for the time that has passed, but never more than the bucket holds.
```

If the bucket then holds less than one whole token, the request is rejected, and the client can be told how long until one token is ready:

```formula reference
W = (1 − b_new) / r
where
W: the wait until the bucket holds one whole token, in seconds; this is the natural Retry-After value
b_new: the tokens in the bucket now, less than 1
r: the refill rate, in tokens per second
In words: the missing fraction of a token divided by how fast tokens arrive. Use this only when fewer than one token remains and the rate is positive. For Retry-After expressed as a delay, round upwards to whole seconds.
```

This executable Python function receives the current token count, its stored timestamp, a trusted current timestamp in seconds, the capacity and the refill rate. Assume finite inputs: capacity at least one, positive refill rate, and a token count between zero and capacity. Use one consistent monotonic clock; never accept arbitrary client timestamps. The small clamp prevents a regressing timestamp from minting tokens, while large forward clock jumps still need an explicit policy.

```python
def take_token(tokens, last_refill, now,
               capacity, rate):
    # Never move stored time backwards.
    now = max(now, last_refill)
    elapsed = now - last_refill
    # Refill only when a request arrives.
    tokens = min(capacity,
                 tokens + elapsed * rate)
    if tokens >= 1:
        # Allowed: spend a complete token.
        return True, tokens - 1, now, 0.0
    # Rejected: keep fractional allowance.
    wait = (1 - tokens) / rate
    return False, tokens, now, wait
```

The returned tuple contains the decision, remaining tokens, new stored timestamp and wait in seconds. The wait is zero for an allowed request; otherwise round it upwards for a whole-second `Retry-After`. This local function does not coordinate concurrent servers; the later atomic-limiter unit handles shared state.

> [!example] Token bucket maths
> Capacity 10, refill 2 tokens/s, bucket full. A client sends 15 requests instantly: the first 10 succeed, 5 get 429. One second later the bucket has 2 tokens, so 2 more can go through. Sustained, the client gets 2 requests/s, or 120 per minute.

The burst and the sustained rate are different limits:

Stored tokens allow a burst above the refill rate. The rate controls sustained average traffic, not a strict cap in every rolling second or minute.

Amazon API Gateway and AWS service APIs use token buckets (they call the parameters "rate" and "burst"). Stripe uses token buckets in Redis.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Refilling admission passes
> **How it maps:** A box holds a limited number of passes and gains new passes steadily. Each visitor uses one. A full box admits a group immediately; later visitors depend on refill.
>
> **Where it stops:** This limiter rejects when no pass remains; it does not queue rejected requests. Real implementations must handle shared state and clock behaviour.

## Key takeaways
- Capacity bounds the stored burst; refill rate sets the sustained average.
- Refill lazily from elapsed time, capped at capacity, then spend a token.
- Round the missing-token wait upwards for a whole-second Retry-After.

## Further reading
- [Stripe blog: Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Wikipedia: Token bucket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Token_bucket)

questions.prompt: A token-bucket limiter rejects requests when empty. After an idle period it refills, capped at its capacity. What happens to requests rejected earlier?

options.text: They are automatically replayed by the bucket.
options.explanation: Rejection does not store a queued request.

options.text: They permanently consume future refill tokens.
options.explanation: The described limiter spends tokens only on accepted requests.

options.text: They force the bucket to remain empty.
options.explanation: Elapsed time refills the bucket independently of rejected work.

options.text: They remain rejected; a client may make a new attempt under its retry policy.
options.explanation: Correct. Refilling permits later arrivals but does not replay old requests.

questions.workedExample: Separate admission control from queueing. A token bucket stores allowance, not pending work. Once it rejects a request, the client must decide whether and when to retry safely. Idle time restores allowance only up to capacity.

questions.prompt: A rejected request needs another 1.6 seconds of token refill, assuming no competing consumption. The server expresses Retry-After as a whole-second delay. Which choice avoids telling the client to return too early?

options.text: Round down to 1 second.
options.explanation: The stated refill would still be incomplete.

options.text: Round up to 2 seconds.
options.explanation: Correct. Whole-second delay syntax requires enough time for the missing allowance.

options.text: Always send 60 seconds.
options.explanation: No full-minute window is part of this token-bucket contract.

options.text: Send 0 because tokens refill continuously.
options.explanation: Continuous refill still takes the stated time.

questions.workedExample: Use the already determined wait, then respect the header’s chosen representation. Rounding down promises readiness too soon; rounding up avoids that error. Other requests or policy changes can still consume the allowance before this client returns.

questions.prompt: A token bucket must allow an immediate burst of 20 requests and sustain about one request per second over time. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Set the refill rate to 20 per second because the burst is 20.
options.explanation: Burst capacity and sustained refill are separate controls.

options.text: Set capacity to 1 because the sustained rate is 1 per second.
options.explanation: That would remove the desired stored burst allowance.

options.text: Use capacity 20 and refill 1 token per second; stored tokens can temporarily exceed the sustained rate.
options.explanation: Correct. Capacity permits a burst while refill bounds the long-run average.

options.text: Use capacity 20 and refill 1 token per second; no interval can ever exceed one request per second.
options.explanation: A full bucket can admit the burst immediately.

questions.workedExample: Capacity answers how much allowance can accumulate. Refill answers how quickly new allowance arrives after it is spent. A token bucket is therefore not the same as a strict rolling-window count, even when its average rate is described per minute.

lessons.title: Leaky buckets and fixed-window boundaries
lessons.summary: Trade queueing delay for smooth output and recognise fixed-window boundary bursts.
lessons.body:
## Leaky bucket

Requests enter a **queue** of fixed size, and are processed (they "leak out") at a constant rate. If the queue is full, new requests are dropped.

```
 requests in (bursty)
     | | |||  |
     v v vvv  v
   +---------+
   | queue   |  size B
   +---------+
       |
       v  constant rate r
   to backend
```

The worst-case extra delay is a full queue draining at the leak rate:

```formula reference
W_max = B / r
where
W_max: an approximate upper bound on queue-drain time, in seconds (s)
B: the queue size, in requests; here 100
r: the leak rate, in requests per second; here 50
s: seconds
In words: a request that joins the back of a full queue waits for every request ahead of it to leak out, so a 100-request queue at 50 per second adds up to 2 s.
```

The output is perfectly smooth, which is great for protecting a fragile downstream (say, a legacy system that can only handle 50 req/s). The cost is latency: bursty requests wait in the queue instead of being served immediately. NGINX's `limit_req` is a leaky bucket; its `burst` parameter is the queue size. Add `nodelay` and queued requests are served immediately instead, while still using up queue slots that drain at the set rate, so the behaviour becomes much closer to a token bucket.

| | Token bucket | Leaky bucket |
|---|---|---|
| Allows bursts | Yes, up to C | No (output smooth) |
| Excess requests | Rejected | Queued, then dropped |
| Adds latency | No | Yes |
| Typical use | Public APIs | Shaping to downstream |

## Fixed window counter

Count requests per client in fixed clock windows: 12:00:00–12:00:59, 12:01:00–12:01:59, and so on.

Use a Redis Lua script so incrementing and assigning the first expiry happen atomically. The application supplies `KEYS[1]`, built from the trusted client identity and current calendar minute, and a validated positive integer limit in `ARGV[1]`. The expiry is a cleanup period from the first request; a different minute gets a different key.

```lua
-- KEYS[1] includes user and clock minute.
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local count = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if count == 1 then
  -- Retain the counter through this minute.
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 60)
end
-- 1 means allowed; 0 means rejected.
return count <= limit and 1 or 0
```

The counter includes rejected attempts too, but only the first request sets its expiry. Redis runs the script without interleaving other commands. Trusted key construction, validated inputs and Redis failure policy are still application responsibilities.

It's extremely cheap: one counter per client per window. But it has a **boundary problem**. With a limit of 100/min, a client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00. That's 200 requests in two seconds, double the intended rate:

Two bursts can straddle a fixed-window boundary: the ending window and the new window each admit their full quota.

```
 limit 100/min
   window 1    |   window 2
 ..........100 | 100..........
          12:01:00
       200 in ~2 s
```

## Key takeaways
- A leaky queue smooths downstream traffic but adds waiting time and drops overflow.
- A fixed-window counter needs little state but can admit two windows’ quota across a boundary.
- NGINX nodelay changes queue behaviour by allowing immediate bursts while slots drain.

## Further reading
- [Cloudflare blog: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)
- [Redis: Rate limiting](https://redis.io/glossary/rate-limiting/)
- [NGINX: Request limiting](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_limit_req_module.html)

questions.prompt: A fixed-window limiter grants a full quota in each calendar minute. A client uses its quota just before the minute changes, then sends another burst just after. What weakness does this expose?

options.text: Both windows can admit their quota, causing a large short burst across the boundary.
options.explanation: Correct. Separate window counts do not enforce the same quota over every rolling interval.

options.text: The new minute must inherit the previous minute’s full count.
options.explanation: That would be a different algorithm; this one resets at the boundary.

options.text: The limiter queues the second burst and releases it smoothly.
options.explanation: A fixed-window counter does not imply a queue or pacing.

options.text: The behaviour occurs only if the counter update races.
options.explanation: Even a perfectly atomic fixed-window counter has this boundary property.

questions.workedExample: The limiter sees two different accounting windows. Each burst can be valid within its own window even though they arrive almost together. Use a rolling count when that is the requirement, or a queue with controlled release when downstream pacing is the objective.

questions.prompt: A legacy mainframe behind your API can handle at most 50 requests/s and falls over with bursts. Clients send bursty traffic averaging 40 req/s. Which algorithm best protects the mainframe?

options.text: Token bucket with capacity 500
options.explanation: A large-capacity token bucket deliberately *allows* bursts of up to 500 requests at once, which is exactly what the mainframe can't handle.

options.text: Leaky bucket (queue) draining at 50 req/s
options.explanation: Correct. A leaky bucket queues incoming bursts and releases them at a constant rate, so the mainframe never sees more than 50 req/s. The trade-off is added latency while requests wait in the queue.

options.text: Fixed window of 3,000 per minute
options.explanation: 3,000/min averages 50/s, but a fixed window lets all 3,000 through in the first second of the minute, which would flatten the mainframe.

options.text: No limiter, because the average is below 50 req/s
options.explanation: The average is fine; the *bursts* are the problem. Without shaping, a spike of 200 in one second will exceed capacity.

questions.workedExample: The mainframe needs paced arrivals, not merely a low average. A bounded queue draining at a controlled rate smooths admitted bursts. Reject excess work when the queue is full and bound queueing delay; otherwise protecting throughput could create unacceptable latency. A large token bucket or minute counter still permits damaging short bursts.

lessons.title: Sliding logs and approximate counters
lessons.summary: Compare exact rolling counts with weighted-window estimates and their burst-sensitive error.
lessons.body:
## Sliding window log

Store a timestamp for every request. On each new request, drop timestamps older than the window and count what's left.

In Redis, a sorted set does this neatly:

```pseudocode
# Remove allowed requests outside the
# window.
ZREMRANGEBYSCORE k 0 (now-60s)
ZCARD k            -> count
if count < limit:
  # A unique member prevents timestamp ties.
  ZADD k now req_id
EXPIRE k 60
```

It's exact, with no boundary problem. But it stores one entry per request in the window:

Memory grows with the number of retained request timestamps. A busy client needs more storage than a quiet one.

As written, the read/count/conditional-add must run in a Lua script, or use `WATCH` with a read followed by `MULTI`/`EXEC` and retry on conflict. `MULTI` alone cannot branch on a queued `ZCARD` result; otherwise two servers can both read `count = 99` and both add.

This version only records *allowed* requests. If you record rejected ones too, a client that keeps hammering stays locked out until it actually backs off, a stricter policy some APIs choose deliberately.

## Sliding window counter

A clever approximation that keeps the cheapness of fixed windows and most of the accuracy of the log. Keep counts for the **current** and **previous** fixed windows, and weight the previous one by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window.

```formula reference
estimate = prev × (1 − t / W) + curr
where
estimate: the approximate number of requests in the last W seconds, compared with the limit
prev: the request count for the whole previous fixed window
curr: the request count so far in the current fixed window
t: the time elapsed since the current window started, in seconds
W: the window length, in seconds (60 for a per-minute limit)
In words: count all of this window's requests, plus an estimated share of the previous window based on remaining time overlap.
```

The weight in the formula is the fraction of the previous window that still lies inside the sliding window: 1 at the start of the current window, falling to 0 at its end.

> [!example] Sliding window counter
> Limit 100/min. Previous minute: 80 requests. Current minute: 30 requests so far, and we're 15 s in, a quarter of the way through. The weighted estimate is 90. That's under 100, so allow. Ten more requests would push it to 100, after which further requests are rejected until the weighting decays.
>
> The weighting decays steadily. At 30 s in, the previous minute counts for half its 80, which is 40, so with 40 requests in the current minute the estimate is 80, leaving room for 20 more.

As the current window advances, less of the previous fixed window overlaps it, so the previous count contributes less.

The approximation assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly. If all 80 arrived in its last second, the true count over the past 60 s is higher than the estimate, the error can be large under adversarial bursts.

Cloudflare described this approach in its 2017 implementation. In that workload’s analysis of 400 million requests from 270,000 distinct sources, only about 0.003% were wrongly allowed or limited.

## Summary

Memory is per client. O(1) means a fixed amount whatever the traffic; B is the leaky bucket’s queue size, n the requests in one window and C the token bucket’s capacity. These are growth classifications, not byte counts.

| Algorithm | Memory | Bursts | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token bucket | O(1) | Up to C | Exact |
| Leaky bucket | O(B) | Smoothed | Exact |
| Fixed window | O(1) | 2× at edge | Poor |
| Sliding log | O(n) | Up to window quota | Exact rolling count |
| Sliding counter | O(1) | Workload-dependent | Approximate; error can be large for clustered arrivals |

## Key takeaways
- A sliding log stores allowed request timestamps and needs an atomic count-and-add decision.
- A sliding counter weights the previous window by remaining overlap.
- Uniform weighting assumes evenly spread arrivals; clustered traffic can cause large errors.
- Historical Cloudflare measurements describe one workload, not an adversarial guarantee.

## Further reading
- [Cloudflare blog: How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)
- [Redis: Rate limiting](https://redis.io/glossary/rate-limiting/)

options.text: The previous window becomes more important.
options.explanation: Its remaining overlap decreases, not increases.

options.text: Its contribution decays, but the estimate is exact only under suitable arrival assumptions.
options.explanation: Correct. Time weighting approximates the distribution within the previous window.

options.text: The estimate reveals the exact timestamp of every old request.
options.explanation: Two counts discard those timestamps.

options.text: The current count must be discarded immediately.
options.explanation: Requests already accepted in the current window still lie within the rolling interval.

A late concentrated burst can make the weighted estimate too low; use a timestamp log if exact rolling counts are required.

Assume the current window has begun but not ended and the previous-window arrivals discussed all remain inside the true rolling window. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.

options.text: It needs only two counters per client, the current and previous windows
options.explanation: True. That's its main advantage over the sliding log, which stores every timestamp.

options.text: It assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly across that window
options.explanation: True. Uniform weighting assumes an even spread. Bursty or adversarial traffic can make the approximation substantially wrong.

options.text: If the previous window’s requests all arrived in its last few seconds, weighting can underestimate the true rolling count
options.explanation: True under the stated timing assumption: all previous arrivals still count in reality, while the approximation discounts them. The excess can be substantial.

options.text: The weight on the previous window equals the fraction of the current window that has elapsed
options.explanation: False: the weight uses the remaining overlap rather than the elapsed fraction. It starts at one and falls to zero as the current window progresses.

options.text: It's exact, like the sliding log, just using less memory
options.explanation: False. It's an approximation. Cloudflare measured the error as tiny in practice (about 0.003% of requests mis-classified), but it isn't zero.

The overlap weight shrinks as time advances, implicitly treating arrivals as evenly spread within the previous window. If they were concentrated near its end and still all lie in the rolling window, that fractional weight undercounts them. A timestamp log can retain the timing needed for an exact count.

lessons.title: Atomic distributed limiters
lessons.summary: Share limiter state and apply refill and consumption atomically without expiry or clock regressions.
lessons.body:
## Distributed rate limiting

With 20 API servers behind a load balancer, a per-server in-memory limiter doesn't work: a client limited to 100/min could get 100 *per server*, or 2,000 in total:

Each independent server grants its own allowance; sharing a client identity does not share its counter.

```
 +----+ +----+ +----+
 |API1| |API2| |API3|
 +--+-+ +--+-+ +--+-+
    \     |     /
     +---------+
     |  Redis  |  shared
     +---------+  counters
```

A common design uses a **shared store** such as Redis for atomic operations and TTLs. Individual command atomicity does not make a multi-command read/modify/write sequence atomic, and failover durability is a separate concern.

## Race conditions

A naïve read-then-write has a race. Two servers both read `tokens = 1`, both allow, both write `tokens = 0`: two requests went through on one token.

Fixes:

- **Atomic commands.** `INCR` is atomic, but the conditional `EXPIRE` must also be protected from a crash between commands, for example by a Lua script. With a separate minute in the key, a missing expiry leaks old keys; with a reused key it can also lock out the client.
- **Lua scripts.** For token bucket, run the whole read-refill-decrement in a Lua script. Redis executes a script atomically, so no other command interleaves.

```lua
-- KEYS[1]=bucket
local C   = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local r   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
-- Missing state starts as a full bucket.
local b = redis.call('HMGET',
  KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or C
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now
-- Never move stored time backwards.
now = math.max(now, ts)
-- Refill and cap before spending one token.
tokens = math.min(C,
  tokens + (now - ts) * r)
local ok = tokens >= 1
if ok then tokens = tokens - 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1],
  'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
-- Expiry must allow a complete refill.
local ttl = math.max(1, math.ceil(C / r))
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ttl)
-- 1 means allowed; 0 means rejected.
return ok and 1 or 0
```

This teaching script assumes a validated finite capacity of at least one token, a positive finite refill rate and a trusted timestamp in seconds. Arbitrary client timestamps must not reach it. Expiry must be no shorter than the time an empty bucket takes to refill completely; otherwise a slow-refilling bucket could expire and incorrectly reset to full:

```formula reference
T_full = C / r
TTL = max(1, ⌈T_full⌉)
where
T_full: the time for an empty bucket to refill to capacity, in seconds (s)
C: the bucket capacity, in tokens
r: the refill rate, in tokens per second
TTL: time to live, how long Redis keeps the key before deleting it, in whole seconds
max: the larger of the two values, so the TTL is never below 1 s
⌈ ⌉: ceiling: round up to the next whole number
s: seconds
In words: keep the key at least as long as a full refill takes; a bucket of 10 refilling at 0.1 tokens per second needs 100 s.
```

Once that time has passed with no requests the bucket would be full anyway, so deleting the key and starting again full gives the same answer.

## Key takeaways
- Independent full-limit counters multiply the reachable fleet quota.
- Atomic commands alone do not protect a multi-command read-modify-write sequence.
- A Redis Lua script can apply refill and consumption without interleaving.
- Retain state for a full refill period and validate capacity, rate and timestamp inputs.

## Further reading
- [Redis: Rate limiting](https://redis.io/glossary/rate-limiting/)
- [Redis: Scripting atomicity](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/eval-intro/)

questions.prompt: Your token bucket limiter runs on 12 API servers sharing Redis. The code does `HGET tokens`, computes the refill in application code, then `HSET tokens`. Under load, clients occasionally exceed their limit by 2–3×. Why, and what's the cleanest fix?

options.text: Redis is eventually consistent. Fix: switch to PostgreSQL
options.explanation: A single Redis primary is linearisable for individual commands. The problem is that a read followed by a separate write isn't atomic, and Postgres would have the same race without explicit locking.

options.text: Clocks on the 12 servers differ. Fix: use NTP
options.explanation: Clock disagreement can itself cause serious refill errors, so it must be controlled. Even with identical clocks, the separate read/modify/write sequence permits the illustrated concurrency race.

options.text: Read-modify-write race: several servers read the same token count before any writes back, so they all allow. Fix: run the whole refill-and-decrement as a Lua script, which Redis executes atomically
options.explanation: Correct. Redis runs each Lua script to completion without interleaving other commands, so read, refill, decrement and write become one atomic step.

options.text: The bucket capacity is too high. Fix: halve it
options.explanation: Capacity only changes how big a burst is allowed. It doesn't fix the race, which lets requests through regardless of the configured values.

questions.workedExample:
Interleave three servers when the bucket holds 1 token:

```
S1: HGET -> 1
S2: HGET -> 1
S3: HGET -> 1
S1: allow, HSET 0
S2: allow, HSET 0
S3: allow, HSET 0
```

One token, three requests allowed. Under high concurrency for one client, this gives the 2–3× overshoot.

Fix with `EVALSHA` on a script that does HMGET → compute → HSET → return. Redis is single-threaded per shard and doesn't interleave commands inside a script, so S2 sees S1's write.

lessons.title: Limiter failures, local shares and placement
lessons.summary: Choose fallback policies, watch shared-store bottlenecks and enforce limits at the appropriate edge.
lessons.body:
## Practical concerns

- **Latency.** Every request now makes a Redis round trip; measure median and tail latency under representative contention.
- **Fail open or closed?** If Redis is down, do you reject everything (closed) or allow everything (open)? A service may **fail open** with a bounded local fallback limiter when availability is more important than temporary quota precision. Local allowances across gateways do not preserve an exact global quota. Security-critical limits (login attempts) may fail closed.
- **Hot keys.** One huge tenant's counter lives on one Redis shard. Shard by client id across a Redis Cluster, and consider local pre-aggregation.
- **Clock skew.** The script above trusts `now` from whichever API server called it. If those clocks disagree, a server whose clock runs behind sees negative elapsed time. Use a trusted shared time source (for example Redis `TIME` in a compatible scripting/replication mode). The sample keeps the stored timestamp from moving backwards; merely clamping elapsed time while storing a lower timestamp can mint extra tokens when time catches up. Large forward jumps still require an explicit clock policy.
- **Approximate local limiting.** At very high scale, each server can enforce its share of the limit locally and sync periodically. It's less precise but needs no per-request network hop. Equal shares need an explicit distribution policy.

Dividing quota equally keeps the combined allocation bounded, but a client concentrated on a few gateways cannot use the shares reserved elsewhere.

> [!note] Measurement gap
> No benchmark establishes Redis latency, bytes per sorted-set member or a universal throughput cutoff here. These depend on deployment and data representation; measured capacity guidance is omitted.

## Where to enforce

Rate limiting usually lives at the **edge**: an API gateway, an Envoy sidecar, or a CDN (Cloudflare, AWS WAF). Enforcing it early means rejected requests cost almost nothing. Finer-grained, per-endpoint limits can live in the application.

Choose the **key** carefully: per API key or user for authenticated traffic; per IP for anonymous traffic (but remember many users can share one IP behind a corporate NAT or mobile carrier).

## Key takeaways
- Measure the shared store’s latency and hot-key behaviour.
- Choose fail-open or fail-closed policies by the protection being provided; local fallback is approximate.
- Equal local quota shares assume evenly distributed client traffic.
- Enforce early and choose identities carefully: many unrelated users share a NAT address.

## Further reading
- [Stripe blog: Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Redis: Rate limiting](https://redis.io/glossary/rate-limiting/)

questions.prompt: A public API handles 200,000 requests/s. Its documented policy favors availability with a bounded local fallback on limiter-store failure, and approximate quotas are acceptable. Which listed choices reduce avoidable storage/coordination cost while preserving useful client guidance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fail open (with a local fallback limiter) if Redis becomes unreachable, for normal API traffic
options.explanation: Correct. A rate limiter is a protection layer; letting a Redis blip turn into a total API outage is usually worse than briefly under-enforcing. A coarse per-server fallback still caps runaway clients.

options.text: Key anonymous traffic only by IP address, with a low limit, without considering NAT
options.explanation: Wrong. Thousands of users behind a corporate NAT or mobile carrier gateway can share one IP. A low per-IP limit would block them all. Combine IP with other signals or use higher limits for anonymous traffic.

options.text: Include remaining-quota headers (`RateLimit`, or `X-RateLimit-Remaining`) on successful responses
options.explanation: Correct. Clients can throttle themselves before hitting 429, which reduces wasted requests on both sides.

options.text: Enforce the limit at the gateway, before requests reach application servers
options.explanation: Correct. Rejecting at the edge means over-limit requests cost almost nothing and don't consume app or database capacity.

options.text: Use a sliding window log for every client, storing every request timestamp
options.explanation: A sliding log may be feasible with sufficient resources, but it retains up to 12 million accepted timestamps for a 60-second window at this rate. Since approximate quotas are acceptable here, constant-state algorithms avoid that storage and churn.

questions.workedExample:
1. Under the stated availability policy, a local fallback can bound some load while accepting reduced quota precision.
2. NAT makes low IP-only limits unfair.
3. Remaining-quota headers help clients adapt; early enforcement avoids app/database work.
4. A 60-second log at 200,000 accepted requests/s retains up to 12,000,000 timestamps. Actual memory depends on representation and key/member sizes; no universal bytes-per-entry estimate is given. Constant-state approximations fit the stated requirement.

questions.prompt: To avoid a Redis hop, each of your 20 gateways enforces an equal local quota share (the client's limit divided by the number of gateways): a 1,000/min client limit becomes 50/min per gateway. A partner's SDK holds two long-lived HTTP/2 connections, so all its traffic lands on just 2 gateways. What happens?

options.text: It's capped at about 100/min, a tenth of its paid limit, because only 2 of the 20 local limiters ever see its traffic
options.explanation: Correct. Local `limit / N` only matches the global limit when traffic is spread evenly across all N servers. Concentrated traffic gets a fraction of its quota.

options.text: It gets its full 1,000/min, because the limits add up across gateways
options.explanation: The limits add up only if traffic reaches all 20 gateways. Two gateways at 50 each is 100.

options.text: It gets 2,000/min, because each gateway lets through up to the full limit
options.explanation: Each gateway enforces 50, not 1,000. Over-allowing is the risk of *per-server full limits*, not of `limit / N`.

options.text: It's blocked entirely, because the gateways disagree
options.explanation: Local limiters don't coordinate, so they can't disagree. Each simply allows up to 50/min on its own.

questions.workedExample: Each gateway owns only its assigned slice. The two gateways serving this client cannot spend quota held by the other eighteen, so the client is limited well below its purchased quota. A shared decision, or a carefully designed allocation/rebalancing scheme, avoids treating local reachability as uniform distribution.

questions.prompt: Your Redis cluster that backs rate limiting becomes unreachable for five minutes. Two limiters use it: a general 1,000/min per-API-key limit on `/v1/*`, and a 5-attempts-per-15-minutes limit on `POST /login`. What's the most defensible behaviour?

options.text: Fail closed for both, so nothing is ever let through without being counted
options.explanation: Rejecting all API traffic because the limiter's store is down turns a protection layer into a total outage, which is usually worse than briefly under-enforcing.

options.text: Fail open for both, because availability always wins
options.explanation: For `/login`, the limit is a security control against credential stuffing. Five minutes of unlimited password guessing is a real risk.

options.text: Fail closed for the general API and open for login
options.explanation: That's backwards: it takes down normal traffic and removes the one limit that defends against attackers.

options.text: Fail open for the general API (ideally with a coarse local fallback limiter), and fail closed, or fall back to a strict local limit, for login
options.explanation: Correct. Match the failure mode to the purpose: the general limit protects capacity, so availability matters most; the login limit protects accounts, so safety matters most.

questions.workedExample:
Ask what each limiter is *for*:

| Limiter | Purpose | If store is down |
|---|---|---|
| `/v1/*` | Capacity, fairness | Open + local cap |
| `/login` | Security | Closed or strict local |

1. A coarse local fallback for the general API (e.g. a per-gateway token bucket) still stops a runaway client from flattening the fleet.
2. For login, a strict per-gateway limit (say 5 attempts per IP per gateway) still slows attackers. Failing closed outright means nobody can log in for five minutes, which may also be acceptable for a short incident.

lessons.title: Sessions, tokens and credential revocation
lessons.summary: Separate identity from permission and compare authoritative session lookups with self-contained tokens.
lessons.body:
Two questions sit in front of every API call:

- **Authentication (authn)**: *who* is calling?
- **Authorisation (authz)**: *are they allowed* to do this?

They're separate concerns and often separate systems. A valid identity does not establish permission for an object. The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) lists broken object level authorisation first: checking login while omitting permission checks for the requested invoice is one example.

## Sessions vs tokens

## Server-side sessions

The classic web approach. After login, the server creates a session record and gives the browser an opaque, random session id in a cookie.

```http
Set-Cookie: sid=9f8c...; HttpOnly;
  Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
```

On each request the server looks up `sid` in a shared store (Redis, a database) to find the user.

- **Session credential revocation applies at validation**: delete that session record and subsequent validated requests using that session are rejected. Other device sessions require separate credential revocation, and cached sessions can delay enforcement.
- **The cookie reveals nothing**: it's just a random pointer.
- **Cost**: a store lookup per request, and the store must be shared across servers (to stay stateless at the app tier).

## Self-contained tokens

The token *itself* carries the claims, signed so the server can verify it without a lookup. JWT is the common format.

- **No lookup**: with asymmetric signing, a service with the trusted public key can verify its signature and then validate its required claims. Great for microservices.
- **Hard to revoke**: without additional credential revocation enforcement, a stolen token remains usable until expiry.

| | Session id | JWT |
|---|---|---|
| Verify | Store lookup | Signature check |
| Revoke | On next authoritative session validation; caches affect delay | Expiry or added credential revocation/status mechanism |
| Size | Chosen random identifier plus encoding overhead | Depends on claims, signature algorithm and encoding |
| Cross-service | Shared authoritative state | Trusted verification key and profile checks |

Neither is universally better. Many systems use **both**: an opaque session cookie at the edge for browsers, translated by the gateway into a short-lived internal JWT for service-to-service calls.

A short-lived access token plus a refresh token checked against current account state narrows the period after an account is disabled. It does not give instant credential revocation: a token issued immediately before disabling can remain valid for its remaining lifetime unless the API enforces a credential revocation mechanism.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Checking a membership list
> **How it maps:** A door attendant who checks the current membership list can reject someone removed from it. An attendant who checks only a still-valid signed pass may admit them until it expires.
>
> **Where it stops:** A token system can add revocation checks or sender constraints. A signature alone does not promise that an account is still enabled.

## Key takeaways
- Authentication establishes identity; authorisation still checks the requested object.
- An opaque session identifier points to server-side state; authoritative validation enforces credential revocation.
- A self-contained token verifies locally but remains valid until expiry unless credential revocation is enforced.
- Short access tokens plus checked refreshes reduce stale-access exposure.

## Further reading
- [OWASP: Session Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [RFC 8725: JWT Best Current Practices](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725)

questions.prompt: An account is disabled at 09:00. Its stateless JWT access token was issued at 08:30 and expires eight hours later. The API validates signature and claims, including exp, but does no credential revocation/account lookup. What exposure remains, and what reduces it without a per-request database lookup?

options.text: No exposure; disabling the account invalidates the JWT
options.explanation: A stateless JWT is verified purely by its signature and claims. The API never consults the account table, so disabling the account changes nothing until expiry.

options.text: Until 16:30. Shorten access tokens to ~10 minutes and use refresh tokens that are checked against the account on each refresh
options.explanation: Correct under the stated validation policy. Short access-token lifetimes reduce exposure to at most about ten minutes if refreshes check the current account state. A jti deny-list can enforce earlier token credential revocation, subject to propagation and cache delays.

options.text: Until 16:30. Switch from RS256 to HS256
options.explanation: Changing the signing algorithm doesn't affect lifetime or credential revocation. It would also make every verifier capable of forging tokens.

options.text: Until 16:30. Rotate the signing key
options.explanation: Issuing a new signing key alone does not invalidate tokens signed by a still-trusted old key. Removing the old verification key from every verifier can invalidate all tokens using it, with propagation/cache delays and broad disruption.

questions.workedExample: A signature and expiry check do not consult the disabled account. Without another credential revocation mechanism the previously issued token remains usable until it expires. Shorter access-token lifetimes bound that exposure, while account checks at refresh stop further tokens being issued. Refresh checks do not revoke already-issued access tokens by themselves.

lessons.title: JWT validation and storage pitfalls
lessons.summary: Treat signed JWT claims as readable and pin algorithms, trusted keys and required claims.
lessons.body:
## JWT in detail

A signed JWT in JWS compact form uses three base64url parts joined by dots. JWTs can also use encrypted JWE forms; this section covers the common signed form:

```
header.payload.signature

{"alg":"RS256","kid":"k1"}
.
{"sub":"user_42",
 "iss":"https://auth.example",
 "aud":"orders-api",
 "exp":1767225600,
 "scope":"orders:read"}
.
<RSA signature over the first two>
```

`exp` is the expiry time as a Unix timestamp, a count of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC: 1767225600 is midnight UTC on 1 January 2026.

The payload is **encoded, not encrypted**. Anyone holding the token can read it. Never put secrets or sensitive personal data in it.

Signing choices:

- **HS256** (HMAC): one shared secret signs and verifies. Every verifier can also *forge* tokens.
- **RS256 / ES256** (asymmetric): the auth server signs with a private key; services verify with the public key, published at a JWKS endpoint. Verifiers can't mint tokens. Prefer this across services.

## JWT pitfalls

RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices) exists because these mistakes keep happening:

1. **`alg: none`.** Early libraries accepted unsigned tokens if the header said `"alg": "none"`. Always pin the expected algorithm on the verifier; never trust the header.
1. **Algorithm confusion.** A server expects RS256 but the library honours the header's `HS256`, then verifies the HMAC using the RSA *public* key as the secret. The attacker, who knows the public key, can forge tokens.
1. **Not validating claims.** Validate the claims required by your token profile, including expiry, issuer and audience, and enforce `nbf` when present. A token issued for `billing-api` must not be accepted by `admin-api`.
1. **Trusting key hints in the header.** `kid`, `jku` and `x5u` tell the verifier which key to use, or where to fetch it. If the verifier fetches keys from whatever URL the token names, the attacker just points it at their own key. Only look `kid` up in your own allow-listed JWKS.
1. **Long lifetimes.** Since you can't easily revoke, choose short access-token lifetimes to bound exposure, and enforce account policy when refreshing. The appropriate lifetime depends on the threat model and credential revocation design.
1. **Storage in the browser.** `localStorage` is readable by any script on the page, so one XSS bug leaks every token. An `HttpOnly` cookie can't be read by JavaScript (though you then need CSRF protection).
1. **Using a JWT as a session.** Stuffing roles into a 24-hour JWT means a demoted admin stays an admin for a day.

> [!tip] credential revocation strategies
> Short access-token lifetime plus a refresh token that *is* checked against a database on each refresh. For urgent credential revocation, keep a small deny-list of `jti` (token id) values until they expire. That's a lookup, but on a tiny, cacheable set.

## Key takeaways
- JWS compact tokens have three encoded parts; signatures provide integrity rather than secrecy.
- Pin accepted algorithms and bind trusted keys to them; never trust arbitrary key URLs.
- Validate the token profile’s issuer, audience, expiry and any not-before claim.
- Short lifetimes, refresh checks and appropriate browser storage reduce theft and stale roles.

## Further reading
- [RFC 7519: JSON Web Token](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519)
- [RFC 8725: JWT Best Current Practices](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725)

questions.prompt: A colleague says: "Our JWTs are safe to put the user's National Insurance number in, because they're signed." What's wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing; a signed JWT is encrypted
options.explanation: Signing and encryption are different. A signature (JWS) proves the token wasn't tampered with; it doesn't hide the contents.

options.text: JWTs can't contain numbers
options.explanation: JWT claims are JSON, so numbers and strings are fine. The issue is confidentiality, not data type.

options.text: The payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone who holds the token (browser extensions, logs, proxies) can decode and read it
options.explanation: Correct. Paste any JWT into a base64 decoder and the claims appear in plain text. Signing guarantees integrity, not secrecy. Keep sensitive data out of tokens, or use encrypted JWTs (JWE) if you truly must.

options.text: Signed JWTs expire too quickly to carry personal data
options.explanation: Expiry is unrelated to confidentiality. Even a token valid for 5 minutes exposes its contents to anyone who sees it, and copies in logs persist far longer.

questions.workedExample:
Decode a JWT payload yourself:

```
eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyXzQyIn0
  base64url decode ->
{"sub":"user_42"}
```

No key needed. A signature only lets the *verifier* detect modification. So:

- Integrity: ✔ (signed)
- Confidentiality: ✘ (not encrypted)

Tokens end up in access logs, browser storage and error reports. Treat the payload as public.

questions.prompt: For signed JWT access tokens whose API profile requires issuer, audience and expiry, which verification practices are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pin the accepted algorithm(s) on the server rather than trusting the token header's `alg`
options.explanation: Correct. Trusting `alg` enables both `alg: none` (no signature at all) and RS256→HS256 confusion, where the public key is misused as an HMAC secret.

options.text: Check that `aud` matches this API
options.explanation: Correct. Without an audience check, a token minted for one service (perhaps a less-trusted one) can be replayed against another.

options.text: Check required `exp` and any present `nbf` against the current time
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise a token stolen months ago still works forever.

options.text: Decrypt the payload with the private key before reading claims
options.explanation: Wrong. A standard signed JWT (JWS) isn't encrypted; verification checks the signature, usually with the *public* key. Decryption only applies to JWE.

options.text: Reject any token larger than 256 bytes
options.explanation: Wrong. An RSA-2048 signature alone encodes to 342 base64url characters, before the header and claims. A size cap is reasonable for DoS protection, but 256 bytes would reject legitimate tokens and isn't a defence against these attacks.

questions.workedExample:
Map each check to the attack it stops:

| Check | Stops |
|---|---|
| Pin `alg` | `none`, alg confusion |
| Validate `aud` | Cross-service replay |
| Validate `exp` | Use of old stolen tokens |
| Validate `iss` | Tokens from a rogue issuer |

'Decrypt with private key' confuses signing with encryption, and a universal 256-byte cap rejects valid tokens. RFC 8725 lists the full set of recommendations.

questions.prompt: Assume a vulnerable JWT verifier trusts the header algorithm and incorrectly permits RSA public-key PEM bytes as an HMAC secret. An attacker sends an HS256 token MACed with those public bytes. What happens, and how should the verifier be fixed?

options.text: It's rejected, because HMAC can't be verified with an RSA key
options.explanation: Vulnerable libraries don't check that the key *type* matches. They treat the PEM bytes as an HMAC secret, and the HMAC verifies.

options.text: It's accepted, because the library computes HMAC-SHA256 with the public key bytes as the secret, which matches. Fix: pass an explicit allow-list, e.g. `algorithms=["RS256"]`, and use a key object bound to one algorithm
options.explanation: Correct. This is algorithm confusion. The public key is public, so the attacker can compute the same HMAC. Pinning the algorithm on the verifier closes it.

options.text: It's accepted, but only until the key is rotated, so the fix is rotating keys daily
options.explanation: The attacker simply re-reads the new public key from your JWKS endpoint and forges again. Rotation doesn't address the flaw.

options.text: It's rejected, because `aud` validation catches forged tokens
options.explanation: The attacker writes the payload, so they set `aud` to whatever you expect. Claim checks only help once the signature is genuinely trustworthy.

questions.workedExample: In this deliberately vulnerable verifier, public key bytes are accepted as an HMAC secret. Anyone with those public bytes can then create the same MAC. Bind trusted keys to the intended algorithm, allow only that algorithm, and validate issuer, audience and required claims. This is a specified misconfiguration, not a claim that current libraries generally permit it.

lessons.title: OAuth delegation and the PKCE code flow
lessons.summary: Trace scoped delegated access and bind an authorisation code to its original client verifier.
lessons.body:
## OAuth 2.0

OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) is a **delegated authorisation** framework. It answers: "how can an app access a user's data on another service *without* being given the user's password?"

Four roles:

| Role | Example |
|---|---|
| Resource owner | You |
| Client | A budgeting app |
| Authorisation server | Google's login |
| Resource server | Gmail API |

The output is an **access token** with limited **scopes** (`gmail.readonly`), which the client sends as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

## Authorisation code flow with PKCE

The recommended flow for any app with a user: web, mobile, single-page apps.

```
User  Client       Auth server   API
 |-tap->|               |          |
 |      | make verifier v          |
 |      | c = S256(v)              |
 |<-redirect /authorize?c--|       |
 |------ login + consent ->|       |
 |<-redirect ?code=xyz-----|       |
 |--code->|                |       |
 |        |-code + v------>|       |
 |        |  check S256(v)==c      |
 |        |<-access+refresh|       |
 |        |-Bearer token---------->|
```

Why the extra steps?

- The **code** travels via the browser (redirect URL), where it might leak: browser history, logs, a malicious app registered for the same URL scheme on mobile.
- The code alone is useless. Exchanging it needs the **code verifier** `v`, a high-entropy random string sent only to the authorization server’s token endpoint, not in the front-channel authorization request. **PKCE** (RFC 7636, "pixy") binds the code to the client that started the flow. The client sends a one-way hash of the verifier, the **code challenge**, at the start (the `S256` method, shown below); the `plain` method (sending the verifier itself as the challenge) gives up most of the protection and shouldn't be used.
- PKCE also stops **authorisation code injection**: an attacker who slips a stolen code into a victim's session can't redeem it, because the victim's client holds a different verifier.
- Tokens return from the token endpoint, not in the redirect URL. A browser-based public client still receives them in its browser process; a BFF can keep them server-side.

The `S256` challenge is computed like this:

```formula reference
c = BASE64URL(SHA256(ASCII(v)))
where
c: the code challenge, sent in the /authorize redirect at the start of the flow and stored by the authorisation server
v: the code verifier: a high-entropy random string of 43 to 128 characters that the client keeps until the token request
ASCII: the ASCII bytes of the verifier string
SHA256: the SHA-256 hash function, which turns any input into a 32-byte digest and cannot feasibly be reversed
BASE64URL: base64url encoding without padding, which writes those 32 bytes as 43 URL-safe characters
In words: the challenge is a one-way fingerprint of the verifier, so seeing the challenge in the browser reveals nothing that lets an attacker redeem the code.
```

At the token endpoint the server recomputes the challenge from the verifier the client sends and compares it with the stored one. RFC 7636's own example: the verifier `dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk` gives the challenge `E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM`. The protection rests on the verifier being long and random: a short or guessable one could be found by trying candidates.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Keeping half of a claim ticket
> **How it maps:** The client keeps a secret verifier and registers its one-way fingerprint. Possessing the returned authorisation code alone is insufficient: redemption must also prove knowledge of that verifier.
>
> **Where it stops:** There is no reversible second half to reconstruct. PKCE does not replace TLS, redirect validation, client authentication where required or protection of the verifier itself.

## Key takeaways
- OAuth delegates access without handing the client the resource owner’s password.
- S256 exposes a one-way challenge while keeping the high-entropy verifier for the token endpoint.
- PKCE protects intercepted and injected codes; browser public clients cannot keep a client secret.
- A BFF can keep issued tokens server-side instead of exposing them to browser JavaScript.

## Further reading
- [OAuth 2.0 overview (oauth.net)](https://oauth.net/2/)
- [oauth.net: PKCE](https://oauth.net/2/pkce/)
- [RFC 9700: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700)
- [RFC 7636: PKCE](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636)

questions.prompt: In the OAuth 2.0 authorisation code flow with PKCE, a malicious app on the same phone intercepts the redirect containing `?code=xyz`. Why can't it obtain an access token?

options.text: Authorisation codes are encrypted with the user's password
options.explanation: OAuth does not require codes to be encrypted with the user's password. In this scenario, protection comes from the matching verifier required at the token exchange.

options.text: The code expires after one second
options.explanation: Codes are short-lived and single-use, but an attacker can act before expiry. OAuth specifies no universal one-second lifetime; expiry alone is not the defence PKCE provides.

options.text: Exchanging the intercepted code requires the original code_verifier; with S256 the server hashes the verifier and compares it with the saved challenge
options.explanation: Correct. The front-channel authorisation request exposes the challenge, not the verifier. A public browser client can hold the verifier itself, but intercepting this code alone does not reveal it.

options.text: The authorisation server checks the attacker's IP address
options.explanation: OAuth doesn't bind codes to IP addresses, and both apps are on the same phone, with the same IP anyway.

questions.workedExample: Before redirection, the client stores a secret verifier and sends only its one-way S256 challenge. On redemption the server hashes the supplied verifier and compares it with that stored challenge. The intercepted code alone lacks the matching verifier. Keep TLS, redirect validation and any required client authentication: PKCE protects this code-binding step.

questions.prompt: You're building a new single-page React app in 2026 that calls your API on behalf of logged-in users through your own OAuth server. Which flow should it use?

options.text: Implicit grant, because SPAs can't keep a client secret
options.explanation: That was the original reasoning for implicit, but returning tokens in the URL fragment exposes them to browser history and page scripts (ordinary HTTP Referer headers do not include fragments). RFC 9700 says not to use it, and OAuth 2.1 removes it.

options.text: Authorisation code with a client secret embedded in the JavaScript bundle
options.explanation: Anything in a browser bundle is public. An embedded secret is readable by anyone who opens dev tools, so it authenticates nothing.

options.text: Authorisation code + PKCE with `S256`, as a public client
options.explanation: Correct. PKCE binds the authorization code to this transaction; it is not client authentication and does not replace a confidential client's secret: only the app instance that created the verifier can redeem the code. Tokens come back over a direct request, not through the URL.

options.text: Resource owner password grant, collecting the password in your own login form
options.explanation: The password grant teaches users to type passwords into apps, and it can't support MFA or federated login. RFC 9700 says it must not be used.

questions.workedExample:
Work through the constraints:

1. A user is present with a browser → a user-facing redirect flow.
2. The SPA is a **public client**: it can't keep a secret.
3. Implicit (tokens in the URL) and password grants are deprecated by RFC 9700 and gone from OAuth 2.1.
4. That leaves **authorisation code + PKCE**, with `code_challenge_method=S256`.

Many teams go one step further with a *backend-for-frontend*: a small server does the OAuth flow as a confidential client and gives the browser only an `HttpOnly` session cookie, so tokens never touch JavaScript.

lessons.title: OAuth grants and refresh-token safety
lessons.summary: Choose machine and device grants, detect refresh-token reuse and apply current PKCE requirements.
lessons.body:
## Other grants

- **Client credentials**: machine-to-machine, no user. A backend authenticates to obtain a token for its own authority, using the configured method such as a client secret, signed assertion or certificate.
- **Device code**: Limited-input devices and CLIs that use a separate browser for approval. The device shows a code; you approve on your phone.
- **Refresh token**: exchange a long-lived refresh token for a new access token. Use **rotation**: each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so reuse of a stolen one is detectable.

> [!warning] Deprecated grants
> The **implicit** grant (access token returned directly in the URL fragment, where it is exposed to browser history and page scripts; fragments are not sent in ordinary HTTP Referer headers) and the **password** grant (client collects the user's password) are out. The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, published as RFC 9700 in January 2025, says the implicit grant should not be used and the password grant must not be. OAuth 2.1 (still an IETF draft, consolidating these rules) drops both grants entirely. Use authorisation code + PKCE instead, including for single-page apps.

## PKCE for every client

PKCE was first designed for *public* clients (mobile and single-page apps) that can't keep a client secret. It turned out to protect confidential clients too, against code injection, which a client secret doesn't prevent.

- **RFC 9700**: PKCE is required for public clients and recommended for confidential ones.
- **OAuth 2.1**: PKCE is required for every client using the authorisation code flow, with only a narrow exception for confidential OpenID Connect clients that use the `nonce` parameter correctly. It also bans the `plain` method and requires exact redirect-URI matching, except for the allowed variable port in native-app loopback redirects.

In practice: use PKCE with `S256` everywhere, and configure your authorisation server to reject code requests without it.

When an invalidated rotated refresh token is presented again, the authorisation server detects possible theft. It cannot tell which participant is legitimate, so revoke the active refresh-token lineage and require a new login. Already issued access tokens need separate credential revocation or expire according to their lifetime. RFC 9700 requires public-client refresh tokens to use rotation or sender constraints.

## Key takeaways
- Client credentials suit machines without a user; device code supports limited-input clients.
- Rotation detects refresh-token reuse; reject the old token and revoke its active refresh lineage.
- RFC 9700 rules and the OAuth 2.1 draft differ in PKCE requirements; use S256 for code flows.
- Implicit and password grants are unsuitable for new deployments under the current security guidance.

## Further reading
- [OAuth 2.0 overview (oauth.net)](https://oauth.net/2/)
- [RFC 9700: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700)
- [oauth.net: OAuth 2.1](https://oauth.net/2.1/)
- [IETF: OAuth 2.1 draft](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1/)

questions.prompt: A nightly batch job in your billing service needs to call your internal reporting API. No user is involved. Which OAuth 2.0 grant fits?

options.text: Authorisation code with PKCE
options.explanation: That flow needs a user to log in and consent via a browser. There's no user in a nightly batch job.

options.text: Implicit grant
options.explanation: Implicit is deprecated and was designed for browser apps with a user. It's wrong on both counts here.

options.text: Resource owner password grant
options.explanation: This grant collects a user's password, which is deprecated and irrelevant when no user exists.

options.text: Client credentials
options.explanation: Correct. The service authenticates as itself with its client id and secret (or a private-key JWT or mTLS) and receives an access token scoped to what the service, not a user, may do.

questions.workedExample:
Decision tree:

```
Is a user involved?
  yes -> has a browser?
           yes -> auth code + PKCE
           no  -> device code
  no  -> client credentials
```

Request:

```
POST /token
grant_type=client_credentials
&client_id=billing
&client_secret=...
&scope=reports:read
```

The token authorizes the billing client under the server's contract; OAuth does not require every access token to be a JWT or contain a sub claim.

questions.prompt: A traditional server-rendered web app is a **confidential** OAuth client with a client secret. You're aligning it with RFC 9700 and OAuth 2.1. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: It should use PKCE too: OAuth 2.1 requires it for confidential clients, apart from a narrow OIDC `nonce` exception
options.explanation: Correct. PKCE is no longer just for public clients. Even where the exception applies, OAuth 2.1 still recommends using it.

options.text: Its client secret already stops a stolen authorisation code being used, so PKCE adds nothing
options.explanation: Wrong. In a code injection attack, the attacker plants a stolen code into the *legitimate* client's callback, and that client redeems it with its own secret. PKCE stops this, because the code is bound to a verifier that client never issued.

options.text: Use `code_challenge_method=S256`, not `plain`
options.explanation: Correct. With `plain` the challenge *is* the verifier, so anyone who sees the authorisation request learns it. OAuth 2.1 prohibits `plain`.

options.text: Because it's confidential, the implicit grant is acceptable for it
options.explanation: Wrong. Implicit is deprecated for every client type. Its problem is tokens in the URL, not whether the client has a secret.

options.text: For this web client, the authorization server should match redirect URIs exactly against registered values
options.explanation: Correct. Pattern or prefix matching has repeatedly let attackers redirect codes to URLs they control. RFC 9700 and OAuth 2.1 require exact string matching.

questions.workedExample:
**Code injection**, step by step, against a client that has a secret but no PKCE:

1. The attacker steals a code issued to the *victim* (e.g. from a leaky log).
2. The attacker starts a login on the real client in their own browser, then swaps the stolen code into the callback.
3. The client redeems it with its own valid secret. The attacker's session is now logged in as the victim.

With PKCE, the code was bound to the victim's `code_challenge`. The attacker's session holds a different verifier, so redemption fails.

The other rules: `S256` keeps the verifier secret, exact redirect matching keeps codes from going astray, and implicit is out for everyone.

questions.prompt: Your auth server rotates refresh tokens. A user's refresh token R1 is stolen. The legitimate app refreshes first, receiving R2 (and R1 is invalidated). An hour later the attacker presents R1. What should the server do?

options.text: Reject R1 and do nothing else, since it has already been used
options.explanation: Rejecting is right, but it wastes the signal. Reuse of a rotated token signals possible compromise (or a duplicate legitimate attempt), and the server can't tell which, so R2 should be distrusted too.

options.text: Accept R1, because refresh tokens are long-lived
options.explanation: Accepting an already-rotated token defeats the entire point of rotation, which is to make each refresh token single-use.

options.text: Issue a new access token but no new refresh token
options.explanation: That still hands the attacker an access token. A rotated refresh token should never produce anything.

options.text: Treat it as theft: reject R1 and revoke the whole token family, including R2, so the user must log in again
options.explanation: Correct for the stated theft scenario: reject reuse and revoke the active refresh-token lineage. Reuse is a compromise signal, though duplicate legitimate refresh attempts can also cause it. Already issued self-contained access tokens need separate credential revocation enforcement or expire naturally.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline:

```
09:00  issue R1
09:05  attacker copies R1
09:30  app uses R1 -> gets R2
       R1 marked used
10:30  attacker uses R1
       -> REUSE DETECTED
       revoke the refresh lineage
       access tokens: revoke separately
       or wait for their short expiry
```

If the *attacker* had refreshed first, the legitimate app's later use of R1 would trigger the same detection. Either way, the reuse is caught and the stolen chain dies. RFC 9700 requires refresh tokens for public clients to be either rotated like this or sender-constrained (e.g. with DPoP or mTLS).

lessons.title: Identity tokens, API keys and sender binding
lessons.summary: Use OIDC identity and API credentials for their intended audiences, with rotatable or sender-bound credentials.
lessons.body:
## OpenID Connect

OAuth 2.0 is about *authorisation*. It doesn't define how the client learns *who the user is*. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an identity layer:

- Request `scope=openid profile email`.
- The token response includes an **ID token**: a JWT with required identity/security claims including `sub`, intended for the *client*. Claims such as `email` and `name` depend on requested scopes, consent and provider behavior and are not guaranteed to be present.
- A standardized UserInfo protocol and discovery document (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`); the UserInfo URL is provider metadata, not a mandatory literal `/userinfo` path.

The distinction matters:

| Token | Audience | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| ID token | The client app | Who logged in |
| Access token | The API | What it may access |

For an OAuth resource API, send the access credential that API requires; an ID token issued to the client app is not a substitute. Follow any other service's explicitly documented token purpose and audience contract. "Sign in with Google/Apple/Microsoft" uses OIDC.

## API keys

For server-to-server integrations, a long random **API key** is simple and common (Stripe's `sk_live_...`, for example).

Good practice:

- **Prefix keys** (`sk_live_`, `sk_test_`) so leaked keys are recognisable, and so secret-scanning tools (GitHub has this) can detect them in public code.
- **Store only a hash** (like passwords), and show the full key once at creation.
- **Scope them** (read-only, specific resources) and allow multiple keys per account so they can be **rotated** without downtime.
- API keys commonly identify a *project or account*; some systems also associate them with users, and are usually long-lived. Never ship a secret key inside a mobile app or browser bundle.

## Mutual TLS (mTLS)

Normal TLS authenticates the server to the client. **mTLS** also makes the client present a certificate, so both sides prove identity at the transport layer.

- Common for **service-to-service** traffic inside a service mesh. Istio and Linkerd issue each workload a short-lived certificate automatically; Istio's identities follow the SPIFFE standard.
- Used by **open banking** and payments partners, in profiles that require certificate-based client authentication.
- RFC 8705 defines **certificate-bound access tokens**: the token is tied to the client's cert, so a stolen token is useless without the private key.
- Where mTLS isn't practical, such as in browsers, **DPoP** (RFC 9449) achieves similar *sender-constraining* at the application layer: the client signs a small proof with its own key on every request.

The main cost is certificate issuance and rotation, which is why meshes automate it.

## Key takeaways
- An OIDC ID token is for the client; use the API’s access credential when calling an API.
- API keys need clear prefixes, hashed storage, scopes and overlapping rotation.
- mTLS authenticates both transport peers and can bind access tokens to certificates.
- DPoP provides application-layer sender constraints where appropriate.

## Further reading
- [OpenID Foundation: How OpenID Connect works](https://openid.net/developers/how-connect-works/)
- [RFC 8705: OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS client authentication](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8705)
- [RFC 9449: DPoP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449)

questions.prompt: A single-page app receives both an **ID token** and an **access token** from an OpenID Connect provider. A developer sends the ID token as `Authorization: Bearer ...` to your orders API. Why is that wrong?

options.text: ID tokens aren't JWTs, so the API can't parse them
options.explanation: OIDC ID tokens *are* JWTs. The API could parse one; the issue is that it shouldn't accept it.

options.text: ID tokens are encrypted and only the browser can read them
options.explanation: OIDC ID tokens are signed and may also be encrypted. Encryption is not what decides whether the orders API should accept one; purpose and audience are the issue.

options.text: It's fine as long as the signature is valid
options.explanation: A valid signature only proves the provider issued it. It doesn't prove the token was intended for, or authorises calls to, this API.

options.text: This ID token authenticates the user to the client app; it is not the access credential issued for the orders API. Use the access token under that API’s validation contract.
options.explanation: Correct. Validate token purpose and intended recipient, not just signature or presence of claims. Access tokens may be opaque or JWTs; their format and audience validation depend on the API’s authorization-server contract.

questions.workedExample:
Illustrative claims for a JWT access-token profile; opaque access tokens need the issuer's validation mechanism:

| Claim | ID token | Access token |
|---|---|---|
| `aud` | spa-client | orders-api |
| purpose | identity | authorisation |
| scopes | not the API authorization credential | `orders:read` |

Your API should validate `aud == orders-api`. An ID token fails that check, and that's the point: any app the user signed into would otherwise get a token usable against your API.
