lessons.title: Object access with roles, attributes and relationships
lessons.summary: Choose RBAC, ABAC or ReBAC while enforcing permission on every requested object.
lessons.body:
## Authorisation models

Once you know who the caller is, decide what they can do.

## RBAC: role-based

Users get **access-control roles**; each role has **API permissions**.

```
alice -> [editor]
editor -> posts:read, posts:write
viewer -> posts:read
```

Simple, auditable and good enough for most internal tools. It strains when permissions depend on context: "editors can edit posts *in their own department*, *during business hours*". Teams end up with role explosion: `editor-uk`, `editor-uk-weekend`...

## ABAC: attribute-based

Decisions are policies over **access-control attributes** of the user, the resource, the action and the environment:

```pseudocode
# Check context and object attributes.
allow if
  user.dept == resource.dept
  and action == "edit"
  and resource.status != "locked"
```

More expressive, but harder to audit ("who can see this document?" requires evaluating policies). Tools such as Open Policy Agent (Rego) and AWS IAM policies are ABAC-style.

## ReBAC: relationship-based

Permissions follow relationships in a graph: "you can view this doc because you're in a group that has access to the folder that contains it". Google's **Zanzibar** (behind Drive, YouTube, Calendar) is the canonical example; OpenFGA and SpiceDB are open-source implementations.

| Model | Best for |
|---|---|
| RBAC | Simple apps, admin tools |
| ABAC | Context-dependent rules |
| ReBAC | Sharing, hierarchies |

Whatever the model, **enforce authorisation on the server for every object**, not just at login, and not just by hiding buttons in the UI.

## Key takeaways
- RBAC groups permissions into roles but can multiply roles for contextual rules.
- ABAC evaluates attributes and environment; ReBAC follows sharing and hierarchy relationships.
- Check object access on the server on every request; a valid token and hidden buttons are insufficient.

## Further reading
- [OWASP API Security Top 10: Broken object level authorization](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/)
- [Google Research: Zanzibar](https://research.google/pubs/zanzibar-googles-consistent-global-authorization-system/)
- [NIST: Attribute based access control](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/attribute-based-access-control)

questions.prompt: A user is logged in with a valid token and calls `GET /invoices/1009`. The API checks the token is valid and returns the invoice, without checking who owns invoice 1009. What class of vulnerability is this?

options.text: Broken object-level authorisation (an IDOR): authentication passed, but authorisation for *this object* was never checked
options.explanation: Correct. A logged-in user can supply another object's id without an object permission check. OWASP lists broken object level authorisation as API1 in its 2023 API Security Top 10.

options.text: Cross-site request forgery
options.explanation: CSRF tricks a victim's browser into making a request with the victim's credentials. Here the attacker uses their *own* valid credentials to access someone else's data.

options.text: Broken authentication
options.explanation: Authentication worked correctly: the server knows exactly who the caller is. The failure is in the authorisation step that follows.

options.text: SQL injection
options.explanation: Nothing is being injected into a query. The query is legitimate; it's just missing an ownership filter.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the two checks:

1. **Authn**: is the token valid? Yes → caller = user 42.
2. **Authz**: may user 42 read invoice 1009? **Never asked.**

Fix: scope every lookup to the caller.

```sql
-- Match the caller as well as the
-- object.
SELECT * FROM invoices
WHERE id = $1
  AND account_id = $caller_account
```

Return 404 if no row, so attackers can't even learn which ids exist. Using unguessable ids (UUIDs) helps but isn't a substitute for the check.

link.title: OWASP API Security Top 10: Broken object level authorization

questions.prompt: A document-sharing product has rules like "you can view a doc if you're in a group that has access to any folder containing it", with nested folders and groups. Which authorisation model fits best?

options.text: RBAC with a role per folder
options.explanation: With thousands of folders and nested groups, you'd need a role per folder per permission, a classic role explosion, while hierarchical RBAC can express inheritance, it may be a cumbersome fit for this resource-sharing graph.

options.text: Relationship-based access control (ReBAC), as in Google Zanzibar, OpenFGA or SpiceDB
options.explanation: Correct. Permissions are naturally a graph: user → member of → group → viewer of → folder → parent of → doc. ReBAC evaluates such paths directly and can also answer 'who can see this?'.

options.text: API keys with scopes
options.explanation: API keys may be associated with accounts or users, but coarse scopes can't express per-document sharing.

options.text: ABAC with only user attributes
options.explanation: ABAC can express rules over attributes, but this rule depends on *relationships* between many entities, which attribute policies represent awkwardly and evaluate expensively.

questions.workedExample:
Write the check as a path:

```
alice --member--> eng-team
eng-team --viewer--> /design
/design --parent--> /design/2026
/design/2026 --parent--> spec.doc
```

Can alice view spec.doc? Walk the graph: yes, via eng-team → /design → /design/2026.

Zanzibar models access using relation tuples. ReBAC directly matches this sharing graph; RBAC with hierarchy or ABAC with suitable relationship data can also model inheritance, so this is a modeling-fit comparison, not a claim of impossibility.

lessons.title: Polling delay and request load
lessons.summary: Compare periodic and held-open requests, accounting for timeout and message-driven completions.
lessons.body:
HTTP was designed for request/response: the client asks, the server answers. But chat messages, live scores, ride locations, stock prices and collaborative cursors all need the **server** to push data to the client the moment it changes.

There are four main techniques, with different directionality, framing and reconnect behavior.

## Short polling

The client asks repeatedly on a timer.

```
Client              Server
  |--GET /msgs?since=t->|
  |<-- 200 [] ----------|
  .. 5 s ..
  |--GET /msgs?since=t->|
  |<-- 200 [] ----------|
  .. 5 s ..
  |--GET /msgs?since=t->|
  |<-- 200 [msg] -------|
```

It's trivially simple and uses ordinary HTTP infrastructure. But it's wasteful and slow:

- **Latency**: for uniformly distributed arrivals and successful punctual polls, the scheduling delay averages half the interval. A 5 s interval gives ~2.5 s average scheduling delay, up to 5 s before adding network and server processing time.
- **Load**: most responses are empty. 1 million clients polling every 5 s is **200,000 requests/s**, nearly all saying "nothing new".

Both follow from the poll interval:

```formula reference
D_avg = I / 2
R = N / I
where
D_avg: the average wait between an update happening and the next poll seeing it, in seconds (s)
I: the poll interval, the time between one client's polls, in seconds
R: the total request rate the server receives, in requests per second
N: the number of clients polling
s: seconds
In words: an update lands at a random point in the interval, so on average it waits half of it; and every client sends one request per interval, so halving the delay doubles the load.
```

These assume updates arrive at random times and every poll goes out on schedule; network and server time add to this scheduling delay.

Short polling is fine for dashboards that refresh every 30–60 s, or job-status checks. It's the right default when updates are rare and a delay is acceptable.

## Long polling

The client asks, and the server **holds the request open** until there's data (or a timeout, typically 20–60 s). As soon as the client gets a response, it immediately asks again.

```
Client              Server
  |--GET /msgs?since=t->|
  |      (held open)    |
  |                     | msg arrives
  |<-- 200 [msg] -------|
  |--GET /msgs?since=t2>|  re-poll
  |      (held open)    |
  |       ...30 s...    |
  |<-- 204 (timeout) ---|
  |--GET /msgs?since=t2>|
```

Updates arrive almost immediately, and there are far fewer empty responses. It uses plain HTTP, but intermediaries still need suitable timeout settings. AWS SQS's `ReceiveMessage` with `WaitTimeSeconds` is long polling.

Drawbacks:

- Each waiting client holds a connection, so large deployments benefit from event-driven I/O or lightweight tasks rather than a dedicated heavyweight OS thread for each idle request.
- There's a small gap between a response and the next request where messages must be buffered server-side, which is why the `since=` cursor matters.
- Each completed poll needs a new request; a response can batch several messages, and HTTP/2 can compress repeated headers.

## Estimating long-poll completions

A held-open request saves empty responses, but does not remove request processing:

Long polls still complete on messages or timeouts. Each completion starts another request, so both message traffic and timeout settings contribute to load.

Shorter timeouts create more empty completions. More frequent messages also complete polls sooner. Batching, network time and reconnect gaps affect measured traffic; size the system with its actual workload.

## Key takeaways
- Short polling trades lower delay for more request traffic.
- Long polls finish on a message or timeout and immediately start another request.
- Buffer messages across re-poll gaps and configure intermediary timeouts.
- Arrival models matter when estimating how often long polls complete.

## Further reading
- [RFC 6202: Known issues and best practices for long polling and streaming](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6202)

questions.prompt: A notification app halves its short-polling interval while keeping the same clients and successful punctual polls. What trade-off should you expect?

options.text: Both delay and request traffic decrease.
options.explanation: Polling more frequently sends more requests.

options.text: Lower scheduling delay, but more request traffic, including empty responses.
options.explanation: Correct. Clients check sooner and more often.

options.text: Instant delivery with no further network requests.
options.explanation: Short polling still waits for the next client request.

options.text: No change because HTTP chooses when the client polls.
options.explanation: The client’s polling schedule sets this trade-off.

questions.workedExample: An update has less time to wait for the next scheduled check. Every client also performs those checks more often, whether anything changed or not. Network and processing time remain additional costs.

questions.prompt: A long-polling server holds a request until new messages arrive or its timeout expires. The client immediately opens another poll after each response. What determines request traffic?

options.text: Both message-driven completions and timeout completions cause new requests.
options.explanation: Correct. Long polling reduces empty responses but does not remove request cycles.

options.text: Only new messages matter; idle clients never send another request.
options.explanation: Idle polls eventually time out and restart.

options.text: Only timeouts matter; messages wait until the timeout.
options.explanation: The server can complete a held request as soon as data is available.

options.text: There is no request traffic after the first connection.
options.explanation: That describes neither the stated long-poll cycle nor its HTTP exchanges.

questions.workedExample: Track one client: a message or timeout finishes its held request, then it polls again. Shorter timeouts increase idle completions; more frequent messages can increase successful completions. Batch size, network time and reconnect gaps affect the actual rate.

lessons.title: Server-Sent Events and replay
lessons.summary: Stream one-way text events with automatic reconnection and a server-backed Last-Event-ID replay path.
lessons.body:
## Server-Sent Events (SSE)

SSE is a standard for the server to **stream** events over one long-lived HTTP response. The browser's `EventSource` API handles it natively.

```
GET /scores/stream HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/event-stream
```

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

id: 101
event: goal
data: {"team":"ARS","min":63}

id: 102
event: goal
data: {"team":"CHE","min":71}
```

Each event is a few text lines followed by a blank line. Features that make SSE pleasant:

- **Automatic reconnection.** If the connection drops, the browser reconnects by itself.
- **Replay of missed events.** On reconnect the browser sends `Last-Event-ID: 102`, so the server can replay anything missed. That only works if the server keeps a short replay buffer (or can query events after id 102); the header just tells it where to start.
- **`retry:` field** lets the server set the reconnect delay.
- It uses HTTP, including HTTP/2 multiplexing. Configure intermediary buffering and timeouts. Native EventSource supports cookies but does not expose arbitrary request headers such as Authorization.

Limitations:

- **One-way**: server to client only. The client sends data with ordinary `POST` requests.
- **Text only** (UTF-8). Binary needs a text encoding such as base64.
- Over HTTP/1.1, browsers allow only ~6 connections per domain, so many tabs with SSE can exhaust them. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams, subject to negotiated stream limits.

SSE suits live feeds, notifications, progress bars and streaming text when the application mainly needs server-to-client updates.

## Key takeaways
- EventSource reads UTF-8 events from a long-lived HTTP response.
- Automatic reconnect does not recover events unless the server retains or can query them.
- Configure buffering, timeouts and connection limits; native EventSource does not expose arbitrary request headers.

## Further reading
- [MDN: Using server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events)

questions.prompt: You're building a live football scores page. Updates flow only from server to browser, a few per minute, to millions of viewers. You want automatic reconnection and replay of missed events after mobile network drops with minimal custom code. Which is the best fit?

options.text: WebSockets
options.explanation: WebSockets would work, but they're full-duplex (you don't need client→server streaming), the browser API has no automatic reconnect, and you'd have to build resume logic yourself.

options.text: Short polling every second
options.explanation: Millions of viewers polling every second means millions of requests per second, nearly all returning no change. Wasteful and still up to 1 s late.

options.text: Server-Sent Events
options.explanation: Correct. SSE is one-way server push over plain HTTP. `EventSource` reconnects automatically and sends `Last-Event-ID`, so the server can replay missed goals. Configure HTTP intermediaries for streaming; native EventSource supports cookies, but not custom Authorization headers.

options.text: gRPC bidirectional streaming
options.explanation: Browsers can't use raw gRPC without gRPC-Web and a proxy, and bidirectional streaming is unnecessary for one-way updates.

questions.workedExample:
Requirements checklist:

| Need | SSE | WebSocket |
|---|---|---|
| Server→client | ✔ | ✔ |
| Client→server stream | not needed | ✔ |
| Auto-reconnect | built in | DIY |
| Resume missed events | `Last-Event-ID` | DIY |
| Plain HTTP infra | ✔ | upgrade needed |

SSE meets every requirement with the least custom code.

questions.prompt: Your SSE notifications stream sends `id:` on every event. A phone drops off the network for 20 seconds during which events 340–352 are sent, then `EventSource` reconnects with `Last-Event-ID: 339`. Users report missing notifications after reconnecting. What's the most likely server-side gap?

options.text: The server ignores `Last-Event-ID` or has nowhere to read past events from, so it only sends new events from the moment of reconnection
options.explanation: Correct. The browser does its half automatically: reconnect and report the last id. The server has to keep a replay buffer (or query a log) and send everything after 339 before resuming live events.

options.text: `EventSource` doesn't reconnect automatically, so the client must do it
options.explanation: It does reconnect automatically; that's one of SSE's selling points. The client did reconnect here and sent the header.

options.text: SSE can't carry ids larger than 255
options.explanation: The `id` field is an arbitrary string. There's no numeric limit.

options.text: The events were binary, which SSE drops
options.explanation: SSE is text-only, but that would fail on every event, not just during the outage. Binary data is sent base64-encoded.

questions.workedExample:
Split the resume work into its two halves:

| Step | Who does it |
|---|---|
| Detect drop, reconnect | Browser |
| Send `Last-Event-ID: 339` | Browser |
| Find events 340+ | **Server** |
| Send them, then go live | **Server** |

Implementation sketch: keep each user's recent events in a capped Redis list or stream (say, the last 5 minutes). Avoid a replay-to-live race: consume a durable stream continuously after the last ID, or establish and buffer a live subscription before replaying to a captured high-water mark, then deduplicate the overlap. If the requested id is older than the buffer, tell the client to do a full refresh.

lessons.title: WebSocket upgrades and duplex protocols
lessons.summary: Trace the classic upgrade and choose a full-duplex transport when clients stream too.
lessons.body:
## WebSockets

A WebSocket (RFC 6455) is a **full-duplex**, persistent connection. It starts as an HTTP request and then upgrades:

```
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
```

```
HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: <accept value>
```

For the shown key, `<accept value>` is `s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=` (the RFC 6455 example).

After the `101`, the TCP connection carries WebSocket **frames** in both directions. Base frame headers occupy 2–14 bytes, excluding extensions and TCP/TLS overhead; fragmented messages use multiple frames. HTTP header sizes depend on the request and protocol version. Text and binary are both supported.

Classic WebSockets take over a whole TCP connection. RFC 8441 defines how to run them as one stream inside an HTTP/2 connection instead, which some browsers and servers support.

Use WebSockets when the client sends frequently too: chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing, trading terminals.

Costs:

- **You build the protocol.** WebSocket gives you a pipe of messages, not semantics. You design message types, acknowledgements, reconnection and resume yourself (or use Socket.IO, Phoenix Channels and similar).
- **No automatic reconnect** in the browser API.
- **Stateful connections** are harder to load-balance and deploy (see below).
- Some corporate proxies still break the upgrade; use `wss://` (TLS) which mostly avoids this.

## Comparison

| | Latency | Direction | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short poll | Half the interval | Pull | Lowest |
| Long poll | Low | Pull-ish | Low |
| SSE | Low | Server→client | Low |
| WebSocket | Low | Both | Higher protocol responsibility |

A practical rule: **SSE for server push, WebSockets when the client also streams, polling when updates are rare.**

## Key takeaways
- Classic HTTP/1.1 WebSocket upgrades with 101, then exchanges text or binary frames.
- WebSocket provides framing; the application owns acknowledgement, reconnect and resume semantics.
- Use SSE for one-way push, WebSockets for frequent two-way streams and polling for rare updates.

## Further reading
- [MDN: The WebSocket API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API)
- [RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)

questions.prompt: Which statements about classic WebSocket over HTTP/1.1 are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The connection starts as an HTTP request with `Upgrade: websocket` and the server replies `101 Switching Protocols`
options.explanation: Correct. The opening handshake is HTTP, which lets WebSockets share ports 80/443 and pass through HTTP infrastructure.

options.text: After the handshake, both client and server can send messages at any time
options.explanation: Correct. WebSockets are full-duplex: neither side has to wait for the other.

options.text: The browser's WebSocket API reconnects automatically after a dropped connection
options.explanation: Wrong. That's a feature of SSE's `EventSource`. With WebSockets you must implement reconnection (ideally with backoff and jitter) yourself or use a library.

options.text: Each message carries full HTTP headers
options.explanation: Wrong. After the upgrade, each base frame header occupies 2–14 bytes, excluding extensions and transport overhead; a message can span several frames. That's a key efficiency advantage over polling.

options.text: WebSockets support both text and binary messages
options.explanation: Correct. Frames have an opcode for text (UTF-8) or binary. SSE, by contrast, is text-only.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through the life of a WebSocket:

1. **Handshake**: HTTP `GET` + `Upgrade` → `101`. (Option 1 ✔)
2. **Data**: frames both ways, any time (option 2 ✔), text or binary (option 5 ✔), tiny frame headers (option 4 ✘).
3. **Drop**: `onclose` fires; nothing reconnects for you (option 3 ✘).

questions.prompt: You're building a collaborative whiteboard. Each user's cursor position is broadcast to everyone else in the room about 20 times a second, and users also send strokes as they draw. Which transport fits best?

options.text: Server-Sent Events, with cursor updates sent as `POST` requests
options.explanation: SSE handles the downstream well, but 20 POSTs per second per user means full HTTP headers on every tiny update. The upstream is as busy as the downstream here.

options.text: Long polling
options.explanation: Without batching, each delivered update completes a poll and requires a new request. Batching reduces requests but adds waiting. It's built for occasional pushes.

options.text: Short polling every second
options.explanation: One-second polling makes cursors jump rather than glide and still sends a request per second per user. It can batch multiple updates, but delivers them in delayed bursts rather than smoothly.

options.text: WebSockets
options.explanation: Correct. Both directions carry frequent, small messages. A base WebSocket frame header adds 2–14 bytes, excluding extensions and transport overhead; HTTP request overhead depends on headers and HTTP version, and either side can send at any time.

questions.workedExample: Both directions carry frequent small updates, so a persistent duplex channel fits the interaction. SSE handles server-to-client events but would need a separate client-to-server request path. Long polling repeatedly completes and reopens requests; slow periodic polling adds visible delay. WebSockets still need application-level flow control, message limits and reconnect behaviour; they do not make the work free.

lessons.title: Connection capacity and cross-gateway fan-out
lessons.summary: Separate durable business state from live connection state and route messages across gateway owners.
lessons.body:
## Scaling persistent connections

Request/response servers are easy to scale because any server can handle any request. Persistent connections break that: each client is attached to *one* server for minutes or hours.

## Connection capacity

An idle connection consumes a socket, buffers, TLS state and application state. Measure memory and active traffic costs for the actual stack; idle capacity does not establish throughput under load.

> [!note] Content gap: connection capacity measurements
> No reproducible benchmark accompanies the generic per-connection memory and per-server capacity estimates previously presented here. Those estimates are omitted; the quiz tests which workloads and resources a capacity plan must cover.

Limits to tune: file descriptors (`ulimit -n`), ephemeral ports on proxies, kernel socket buffers and TLS memory.

## The fan-out problem

Alice is connected to gateway A. Bob is on gateway C. Alice sends Bob a message. How does gateway A get it to C?

```
Alice        Bob
  |           |
+---+ +---+ +---+
| A | | B | | C |  WS gateways
+-+-+ +---+ +-+-+
  |  pub   sub|
  v           |
+---------------+
| pub/sub layer |
| Redis / Kafka |
+---------------+
```

The usual architecture:

1. **Gateway tier** that owns connection state while durable business state lives in services or storage. Keeping business logic separate can simplify scaling.
1. A **connection registry** mapping `user → gateway` (in Redis), or a **pub/sub** channel per user, room or topic.
1. Business logic in ordinary services, which publish messages; the gateway subscribed for that user or channel delivers them.

Slack's real-time architecture works like this: channel servers hold state for channels, gateway servers hold the WebSocket connections, and messages are routed between them. Socket.IO's Redis adapter does the same at small scale, using Redis pub/sub to broadcast across nodes.

For memory sizing, first reserve the OS/runtime allocation, divide the remaining memory by measured memory per connection, apply the target utilisation headroom, then divide the required client count by that per-server allowance and round the server count upwards. CPU, file descriptors and reconnect handshakes may constrain the deployment earlier.

## Key takeaways
- Measure per-connection costs and allow capacity headroom; idle capacity does not establish active throughput.
- A registry or pub/sub layer reaches clients attached to other gateways.
- Keep durable business state in services or storage while gateways own connection state.

## Further reading
- [Slack engineering: Real-time messaging](https://slack.engineering/real-time-messaging/)
- [Discord: How Discord scaled Elixir to 5,000,000 concurrent users](https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-scaled-elixir-to-5-000-000-concurrent-users)
- [Socket.IO: Redis adapter](https://socket.io/docs/v4/redis-adapter/)

questions.prompt: A chat service has 20 WebSocket gateway servers behind a load balancer. Alice (on gateway 3) sends a message to a group whose members are spread across 12 gateways. What's the standard way to deliver it?

options.text: Use sticky sessions so all group members end up on the same gateway
options.explanation: Group members connect independently from all over the world. You can't force thousands of users into one server, and a user in many groups can only be on one gateway.

options.text: Gateway 3 opens a direct connection to every other gateway and broadcasts
options.explanation: A full mesh of N² connections that sends every message to every gateway, even those with no members, doesn't scale and couples gateways tightly.

options.text: Members poll a REST endpoint for new group messages
options.explanation: That throws away the point of having WebSockets and reintroduces polling load and latency.

options.text: The message is published to a pub/sub channel for the group (for example, Redis Pub/Sub; Kafka needs explicit consumer-group and routing design); each gateway holding a member's connection is subscribed and pushes it down to its local sockets
options.explanation: Correct. Gateways stay stateless apart from connections, targeted subscriptions can route to interested gateways. Slack uses channel/gateway routing; Socket.IO's standard Redis adapter broadcasts between nodes and does not guarantee this exact selective-delivery topology.

questions.workedExample:
```
Alice -> GW3 -> chat service
  1. persist message
  2. PUBLISH group:42 msg

GW1, GW5, ... (12 of 20)
  SUBSCRIBEd to group:42
  -> push to local members
```

Key properties:
- Only the 12 gateways with members get the message (not all 20).
- Gateways subscribe when a member connects and end that subscription when the last one leaves.
- Persisting first means offline members can fetch it later. Use an outbox or equivalent recovery mechanism so a crash between persistence and publish does not permanently suppress live delivery.

Messaging systems themselves are covered in the messaging module.

questions.prompt: A WebSocket gateway has enough RAM for its expected idle connections. Why is that not yet a complete capacity plan?

options.text: Idle connections consume no other resources.
options.explanation: They still need operating-system resources and can become active or reconnect.

options.text: More RAM guarantees unlimited message throughput.
options.explanation: CPU, network bandwidth, queues and dependencies can limit active traffic.

options.text: Allow headroom and test messages, handshakes, authentication and failure redistribution as well as memory.
options.explanation: Correct. An idle-memory estimate covers only one workload and resource.

options.text: The number of connections alone determines every server cost.
options.explanation: Message rates and behaviour per connection can differ greatly.

questions.workedExample: Measure idle connection memory, then test the active workload. Reconnect bursts can stress TLS and authentication, while message fan-out stresses CPU and network capacity. Reserve room for a failed gateway’s clients to move elsewhere; a memory-only division cannot establish safe fleet size.

lessons.title: Heartbeats, draining and reconnect budgets
lessons.summary: Keep persistent connections alive and rebalance or deploy without overwhelming reconnect dependencies.
lessons.body:
A fleet with enough memory can still fail during deploys: reconnecting clients consume authentication and handshake capacity. Plan for connection turnover as well as steady state.

## Load balancing

- The load balancer must support the `Upgrade` and long-lived connections. L7 balancers such as NGINX, Envoy and AWS ALB do. Set idle timeouts generously (AWS ALB's default is 60 s) and send **heartbeats** (ping/pong) every ~30 s, so that idle connections aren't culled by the balancer or by NAT devices along the way.
- Heartbeats also detect *dead* connections. A phone that loses signal doesn't send a TCP close, so without pings the server can hold a "connected" socket for a client that vanished minutes ago.
- Balancing happens at **connect** time only. If you add servers, existing connections stay where they are, so new servers initially receive only new or reconnected clients. Use least-connections balancing, and consider a maximum connection age (say, a few hours, with jitter) so the fleet rebalances itself gradually.

## Deploys and reconnect storms

Restarting a gateway drops every connection on it at once. If 200,000 clients all reconnect immediately, they hammer the auth service and the remaining gateways.

- **Drain gracefully**: stop accepting new connections, then close existing ones gradually over minutes.
- **Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter**.
- **Resume, don't replay everything**: the client sends its last-seen message id or sequence number, and the server sends only what was missed.

## Managed options

If you don't want to run this yourself: AWS API Gateway WebSocket APIs, Azure Web PubSub, Ably, Pusher. They hold the connections and give your backend a simple "send to connection id" API.

If each reconnect makes one auth call, the drain cannot close connections faster than the spare authentication throughput can accept them. Divide the connections being moved by spare calls per second to obtain an ideal minimum drain duration, then allow extra time for variability and simultaneous fleet work.

## Key takeaways
- Heartbeat cadence must suit idle timeouts and also detects clients that vanished.
- New servers receive new connections; existing connections require gradual reconnection to rebalance.
- Drain gradually within auth capacity, and use client backoff and jitter.
- Resume from last-seen identities and consider managed gateways when operating the fleet is unnecessary.

## Further reading
- [Slack engineering: Real-time messaging](https://slack.engineering/real-time-messaging/)
- [Discord: How Discord scaled Elixir to 5,000,000 concurrent users](https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-scaled-elixir-to-5-000-000-concurrent-users)
- [AWS: Load balancer idle timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-load-balancer-attributes.html)

questions.prompt: You deploy a new version to a WebSocket gateway holding 200,000 connections by killing the process. Within seconds, your auth service falls over. Why, and what are the best mitigations?

options.text: All 200,000 clients reconnect at once, each re-authenticating: a thundering herd. Drain gradually, reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and resume from the last-seen sequence number
options.explanation: Correct. Killing the process drops every connection simultaneously, and naïve clients reconnect immediately. Gradual draining spreads the load over minutes, jitter de-synchronises clients, and resume avoids a full state reload.

options.text: The new version uses a different WebSocket protocol version
options.explanation: WebSocket version 13 has been stable since 2011. A protocol mismatch would cause handshake failures, not an auth-service overload.

options.text: Long-lived connections leak memory in the auth service
options.explanation: Auth isn't holding the WebSocket connections; the gateway is. The auth load comes from the burst of new handshakes.

options.text: The load balancer can't route WebSockets after a deploy
options.explanation: The LB keeps routing fine; it's the sudden volume of reconnects, not routing, that causes the failure.

questions.workedExample: Killing a gateway disconnects its entire population together. Their reconnects repeat TLS and authentication work, which can overload shared dependencies. Stop admitting new connections, drain in stages, spread client retries with jitter and resume from a retained sequence when supported. Coordinate the fleet’s drains against the capacity of the services that accept reconnects.

questions.prompt: Your WebSocket fleet has 10 gateways, each with about 100,000 connections. During a traffic spike you add 10 more. An hour later the new gateways have only a few thousand connections each and the old ones are still overloaded. Which actions help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use least-connections balancing, so new connections prefer the emptier gateways
options.explanation: Correct. Round-robin would send only half of new connections to the new gateways; least-connections sends nearly all of them there until the fleet evens out.

options.text: Have overloaded gateways gradually close a slice of connections, asking clients to reconnect with jittered backoff
options.explanation: Correct. Connections only move when clients reconnect. Closing a controlled slice, slowly, lets them land on the new gateways without a reconnect storm.

options.text: Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer
options.explanation: Stickiness tries to send a client back to the *same* gateway, which is the opposite of what you need here.

options.text: Set a maximum connection age with jitter, so connections naturally recycle over time
options.explanation: Correct. A max age (e.g. a few hours ± random) means the fleet keeps rebalancing on its own, including after future scale-outs.

options.text: Restart the old gateways all at once so every client reconnects
options.explanation: That moves the connections, but 1 million simultaneous reconnects hammer auth and the gateways: a self-inflicted thundering herd.

questions.workedExample:
1. The root cause: balancing happens only at **connect** time. Existing connections stay where they were.
2. To fix it, you need *new* connections to go to the right place, and *some* old connections to become new ones:
   - least-connections → new connects go to new gateways ✔
   - gradual, jittered shedding → old connects move, slowly ✔
   - max connection age → continuous rebalancing ✔
3. Moving all of them at once is the reconnect-storm failure mode. ✘
4. Stickiness is for keeping clients where they are. ✘

Target: 1,000,000 connections across 20 gateways = 50,000 each.

questions.prompt: Your chat app's WebSocket connections run through an AWS Application Load Balancer with its default settings. Users in quiet rooms keep getting disconnected roughly every minute, but busy rooms are fine. What's the fix?

options.text: Switch from WebSockets to short polling
options.explanation: That throws away the real-time design to work around a timeout setting. It would also add far more load than the occasional ping.

options.text: Send WebSocket ping/pong heartbeats every ~30 s (and/or raise the ALB idle timeout), so idle connections never look idle
options.explanation: Correct. The ALB closes connections with no traffic for its idle timeout, 60 s by default. Quiet rooms send nothing for a minute; busy rooms always have traffic. Heartbeats keep the connection active and also detect dead clients.

options.text: Enable sticky sessions
options.explanation: A WebSocket is already one long-lived connection to one target. Stickiness affects where *new* requests go, not idle timeouts.

options.text: Use binary frames instead of text frames
options.explanation: The frame type doesn't matter. The connection is being closed because no frames of any kind are flowing.

questions.workedExample:
Read the clue: **quiet** rooms disconnect, **busy** rooms don't, at about **60 s** intervals.

1. Something closes connections after ~60 s of silence.
2. AWS ALB's default idle timeout is 60 s.
3. Busy rooms reset the idle timer with every message; quiet rooms don't.

The same pings let the server notice clients that vanished without closing the socket (a phone losing signal), so it can free their resources.

lessons.title: Webhook signatures and replay defences
lessons.summary: Authenticate raw delivery bytes, rotate secrets safely and reject stale or repeated signed payloads.
lessons.body:
The previous lesson covered pushing data to *browsers*. Webhooks push data to *other servers*: Stripe tells your backend a payment succeeded, GitHub tells your CI that code was pushed, Shopify tells your app an order was placed.

Later units cover delivery, ordering and the gateways and backends-for-frontends that sit in front of APIs.

## Webhooks: reverse APIs

A webhook is an HTTP `POST` that **the provider** sends to a URL **the consumer** registered. It's an API call in the opposite direction.

```
Provider            Your server
(Stripe)            /webhooks/stripe
   |                     |
   | payment succeeded   |
   |--- POST event ----->|
   |                     | verify sig
   |                     | enqueue
   |<----- 200 OK -------|
   |                     | process async
```

A typical delivery:

```
POST /webhooks/stripe HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Stripe-Signature: t=1767225600,
  v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32a...

{"id": "evt_1Nq...",
 "type": "payment_intent.succeeded",
 "created": 1767225600,
 "data": {"object": {...}}}
```

The alternative is the consumer polling `GET /events?since=...`. Webhooks are more efficient and faster, but they shift a lot of reliability problems onto both sides.

## Problem 1: authenticity

Your webhook URL is public. Anyone who discovers it can `POST` a fake "payment succeeded" event and get free goods. You must verify that each request genuinely came from the provider.

A common technique is an **HMAC signature** (a shared-secret message authentication code). Follow the provider-specific signing protocol; asymmetric signatures are another option. Provider and consumer share a secret (`whsec_...`). The provider computes (this is Stripe's scheme):

```formula reference
m = t + "." + b
sig = HMAC(k, m)
where
m: the signed message: the bytes the signature covers
t: the timestamp of the delivery, as a Unix timestamp in seconds
b: the raw request body, exactly the bytes sent
+: joined end to end (concatenation), not addition
k: the shared webhook secret
HMAC: HMAC-SHA256, a keyed hash that only someone holding k can compute; it outputs 32 bytes, sent as 64 hex characters
sig: the signature
In words: glue the timestamp, a dot and the raw body together, then hash that with the shared secret.
```

and sends `t=<timestamp>,v1=<sig>` in a header. For the delivery above, the signed message is `1767225600.` followed by the exact body bytes. The consumer recomputes the HMAC and compares. In Python:

```python
import hashlib, hmac

def sign(secret, t, raw_body):
    # Bind the timestamp to exact body
    # bytes.
    msg = t.encode() + b"." + raw_body
    # Hex is the signature header value.
    return hmac.new(secret, msg,
        hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
```

Details that matter:

- **Use the raw body bytes.** If your framework parses and re-serialises the JSON first, whitespace or key order changes and the signature won't match.
- **Compare in constant time** (`hmac.compare_digest`, `crypto.timingSafeEqual`). Ordinary equality checks are not guaranteed constant-time and can expose timing differences; use a vetted constant-time comparison for appropriately validated equal-length inputs.
- **Support multiple secrets during rotation.** Stripe and the Standard Webhooks spec allow several signatures in one header so old and new secrets both verify during the changeover.

GitHub uses `X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<hmac>`, computed over the body alone, with no timestamp. The **Standard Webhooks** specification (backed by Svix, Zapier, Twilio and others) standardises `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp` and `webhook-signature` headers, and signs `id.timestamp.body`, so the message id and timestamp are both covered.

## Problem 2: replay attacks

An attacker who captures one genuine, correctly signed webhook (from a log, a misconfigured proxy) can resend it later. The signature is still valid.

Defences:

- **Sign the timestamp** along with the body (as above), and **reject events whose timestamp is too old**. Stripe's libraries default to a 5-minute tolerance. The check is shown below this list.
- **Deduplicate by event id.** Store processed `evt_...` ids and ignore repeats. You need this anyway for retries (below). For GitHub, `X-GitHub-Delivery` is useful for ordinary redelivery deduplication, but it is not included in the body HMAC: someone replaying a captured body can change that header. Use authenticated payload identity or a retained digest of the verified raw body where appropriate, make business effects idempotent, and reconcile current provider state. Without signed freshness or retained identity, the signature alone cannot reject an old valid payload.

An age check rejects old deliveries after signature verification. Follow the provider SDK's clock-skew policy as well; an old-age test alone does not reject future timestamps.

For example, a delivery signed 15 minutes ago fails a five-minute age tolerance even if its signature is valid. A valid signature proves authenticity of the signed bytes, not freshness by itself.

> [!warning] Why the timestamp must be inside the signature
> If the timestamp were sent separately and unsigned, an attacker could replay an old body with a fresh timestamp. Including it in the signed string means changing it breaks the signature.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A dated authenticated notice
> **How it maps:** Authenticating the date together with a notice prevents an attacker changing an old notice to look newly issued. A separate record of notice identities helps detect repeats still inside the allowed age.
>
> **Where it stops:** An HMAC uses a shared secret, so either secret holder can compute it. It does not encrypt the notice or prove that the business event has not already been handled.

## Key takeaways
- A webhook is a provider-to-consumer HTTP notification whose public endpoint must authenticate each request.
- Sign the provider-defined raw bytes and compare with a vetted constant-time function.
- Signed freshness and retained authenticated identity solve different replay cases.
- Use overlapping signatures during supported secret rotation; unsigned delivery identifiers cannot prove freshness.

## Further reading
- [Stripe docs: Verify webhook signatures](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks/signature)
- [GitHub docs: Validating webhook deliveries](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/validating-webhook-deliveries)
- [Standard Webhooks specification](https://github.com/standard-webhooks/standard-webhooks/blob/main/spec/standard-webhooks.md)

questions.prompt: Your `/webhooks/payments` endpoint marks orders as paid when it receives a `payment.succeeded` event. It doesn't verify signatures. What's the main risk?

options.text: Events might arrive slowly
options.explanation: Latency is a reliability concern, not the main risk here. The bigger problem is that the endpoint trusts anything it receives.

options.text: The provider will stop sending events
options.explanation: Providers don't know or care whether you verify signatures; deliveries continue either way.

options.text: Duplicate events will double-mark orders
options.explanation: Duplicates are a real concern, but they're solved by deduplicating on event id, not by signatures. And marking an order paid twice is usually harmless.

options.text: Anyone who discovers the URL can POST a forged event and get orders marked as paid without paying
options.explanation: Correct. Without the provider's required authentication mechanism, this public endpoint cannot distinguish the forged request. HMAC is one common mechanism; other authenticated delivery schemes exist.

questions.workedExample: An attacker can submit a correctly shaped but invented payment event to a public URL. Without the provider’s authentication check, the handler has no basis to treat it as authentic. Verify the exact signed bytes with the appropriate key before trusting the content, then separately handle freshness, duplicate identity and business state.

questions.prompt:
Your Stripe-style `timestamp.body` signature check fails on genuine deliveries even though the secret is correct. This Python function receives the decoded secret bytes, ASCII timestamp bytes and raw body bytes:

```python
import hmac, json

def wrong_signature(secret, ts, raw):
    # Parsing loses the original layout.
    body = json.loads(raw)
    # Re-encoding cannot restore it.
    payload = json.dumps(body).encode()
    msg = ts + b"." + payload
    return hmac.digest(secret, msg,
                       "sha256")
```

What is the most likely bug?

options.text: HMAC-SHA256 can't sign JSON
options.explanation: HMAC signs arbitrary bytes. JSON is fine, as long as you sign exactly the bytes that were sent.

options.text: The body is parsed and re-serialised, so whitespace, key order or escaping differ from the raw bytes the provider signed
options.explanation: Correct. Even one changed space produces a completely different HMAC. Always verify against the raw request body before any parsing.

options.text: The timestamp should come after the body
options.explanation: The order is set by the provider's spec. Stripe uses `timestamp.body`, which this code follows. The problem is the body bytes themselves.

options.text: The secret must be base64-decoded first
options.explanation: Some providers (Standard Webhooks) do use base64 secrets, but the question says the secret is correct. The re-serialisation bug would break verification regardless.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the body bytes:

```
sent:   {"id": "evt_1",  "amt":5}
re-ser: {"id": "evt_1", "amt": 5}
```

Re-serialisation changes the signed byte sequence, so the digest no longer matches, apart from cryptographically negligible collisions. Preserve the original bytes and compare the computed digest with the supplied, decoded 32-byte signature:

```python
import hmac, json

def parse_if_signed(secret, ts, raw,
                    sig):
    # Preserve the provider's bytes.
    msg = ts + b"." + raw
    expected = hmac.digest(secret, msg,
                           "sha256")
    # sig is a decoded 32-byte digest.
    if not hmac.compare_digest(
            expected, sig):
        raise ValueError("bad HMAC")
    return json.loads(raw)
```

With a matching digest, this fixture returns the parsed event. Changing the raw body while keeping that digest raises `ValueError`. This is **signature-only pedagogy**: it does not validate freshness, header encodings, secret selection, delivery identity or duplicate effects. Use the provider SDK and its current signing/freshness contract in a real handler. Stripe signs the timestamp and body; GitHub’s different protocol signs the body alone.

questions.prompt: An attacker captures a genuine, correctly signed `refund.created` webhook from a misconfigured log and resends it to your endpoint 2 hours later. Your code verifies the HMAC over `timestamp.body` and allows a 5-minute tolerance. What happens?

options.text: It's rejected, because the signed timestamp is 2 hours old, beyond the 5-minute tolerance, and the attacker can't change the timestamp without invalidating the signature
options.explanation: Correct. Because the timestamp is part of the signed string, the attacker must either send the old timestamp (rejected as stale) or a new one (signature mismatch).

options.text: It's accepted, because the signature is valid
options.explanation: The signature is valid only for that exact timestamp. The tolerance check is what makes a valid-but-old signature useless.

options.text: It's accepted, but only if the attacker updates the timestamp header
options.explanation: Updating the timestamp changes the signed string, so the recomputed HMAC no longer matches the captured signature.

options.text: It depends on whether the event id was already processed; timestamps don't help
options.explanation: Deduplication by event id is a second, complementary defence, but the timestamp check alone already rejects this replay.

questions.workedExample:
Attacker's two options:

| Send | HMAC check | Age check |
|---|---|---|
| Old `t` | ✔ match | ✘ 2 h > 5 min |
| New `t` | ✘ mismatch | (n/a) |

Either way, rejected.

Within the 5-minute window a replay could still pass the timestamp check, which is why you also dedupe on the event id: belt and braces.

questions.prompt: You consume GitHub webhooks and verify `X-Hub-Signature-256` correctly. GitHub's HMAC covers only the body; there's no signed timestamp. An attacker captures one genuine `push` delivery and replays it a day later. What's your main defence?

options.text: Reject deliveries older than 5 minutes using the `Date` header
options.explanation: The `Date` header isn't part of the signature, so the attacker can set it to anything. An unsigned timestamp proves nothing.

options.text: None is needed: a valid signature proves the delivery is fresh
options.explanation: A signature proves the body came from GitHub at *some* point. A replayed copy has the same valid signature, which is exactly why replays are dangerous.

options.text: Rotate the webhook secret every day
options.explanation: Rotation limits how long one captured delivery stays valid, but it's operationally painful and still leaves a window. It isn't the primary defence.

options.text: Use authenticated payload identity or a retained digest of verified raw bytes for replay detection, and make business effects idempotent; the unsigned delivery header alone is insufficient
options.explanation: Correct. A captured body remains authentically signed. Retained authenticated identity can detect repeats; reconcile current provider state for stale events. The attacker can replace X-GitHub-Delivery without invalidating the body HMAC.

questions.workedExample:
1. Replay protection needs something the attacker can't change: either a **signed** timestamp or a record of what you've already seen.
2. GitHub signs only the body, so any timestamp in a header is unprotected.
3. That leaves **deduplication**: retain authenticated event identity or the verified body digest where suitable; the unsigned delivery id only helps ordinary redelivery deduplication.
4. An attacker could change the unsigned delivery id, so also make processing idempotent on the *content*, e.g. define a business key including the repository, ref and commit for the intended effect, so an unrelated repository or legitimate new operation is not accidentally suppressed.

Compare with Stripe and Standard Webhooks, which put the timestamp inside the signed string, so stale replays are rejected outright.

questions.prompt: You need to rotate a webhook signing secret. The provider and your 30 consumer servers can't switch at the same instant. How do you avoid rejecting genuine webhooks during the changeover?

options.text: Turn off signature verification for the rotation window
options.explanation: That opens exactly the window an attacker would want, and there's no need for it.

options.text: Have the provider sign each delivery with both old and new secrets during an overlap period, and have consumers accept a delivery if any signature matches a secret they hold
options.explanation: Correct. Stripe and Standard Webhooks both allow several signatures in one header for this reason. Consumers can roll forward one at a time, then the old secret is retired.

options.text: Return 500 for failed signatures, so the provider retries until the new secret is everywhere
options.explanation: That relies on retry timing to paper over the gap, delays every event, and may exhaust the retry schedule. Overlapping secrets avoid the failures in the first place.

options.text: Encrypt the old secret with the new one
options.explanation: That has no effect on verification. The consumer still needs to check a signature made with a secret it holds.

questions.workedExample:
A safe rotation has an overlap where both secrets are valid:

```
T0  provider: sign with old
T1  provider: sign with old+new
    header: v1=<old>,v1=<new>
T2  consumers roll out new
    (accept either)
T3  provider: sign with new
T4  consumers drop old
```

At every moment, each delivery carries at least one signature that every consumer can verify. No window without verification, and no rejected events.

lessons.title: Durable webhook processing and retries
lessons.summary: Acknowledge persisted events quickly, deduplicate effects and isolate provider delivery workloads.
lessons.body:
A valid notification can still be duplicated, delayed or missed. Treat signature verification as the start of a durable processing path, then account for both consumer and provider failures.

## Problem 3: delivery failures and retries

Your endpoint will sometimes be down, slow or buggy. Many providers retry failed delivery with backoff, so duplicates are possible. Bounded retry windows do not guarantee that every event is eventually delivered. Stripe retries for up to **3 days** in live mode (far less in test mode); GitHub doesn't retry failed deliveries automatically, but lets you redeliver them from the UI or API.

What this means for you as a consumer:

- **Respond 2xx quickly**, within a few seconds. Providers time out (GitHub asks for a 2xx within 10 seconds) and treat slow responses as failures. Providers with automatic retries can then send duplicates; GitHub instead supports explicit redelivery.
- **Do the work asynchronously.** Verify the signature, write the event to a queue or table, return `200`, then process. Your downstream outage then doesn't become a webhook failure.
- **Be idempotent.** The same event may arrive more than once. Deduplicate on the authenticated event identity, in the same transaction as a local database side effect. External effects need downstream idempotency or reconciliation; a local transaction cannot atomically commit a remote API call.

This SQL fragment needs the actual order predicate and a branch on the inserted-row count. The following is transaction pseudocode, not a complete handler.

```sql
BEGIN;
-- Commit event identity with its local
-- effect.
INSERT INTO processed_events(id)
  VALUES ('evt_1Nq')
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
-- if 0 rows inserted: duplicate,
--   COMMIT and return
UPDATE orders SET paid = true ...;
COMMIT;
```

As a **provider**, you need:

- A durable outbox of events, a delivery worker pool, and per-endpoint retry schedules (e.g. 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 8 h...).
- **Auto-disable** endpoints that fail for days, and email the owner.
- **Isolation** between customers, so one customer's slow endpoint doesn't block deliveries to everyone else.
- An **events API** (`GET /events`) so consumers can reconcile anything missed. Webhooks should be a notification channel, not the only source of truth.

## Key takeaways
- Persist a verified event before acknowledging, then process asynchronously.
- Commit local deduplication with the effect; remote effects need their own protection.
- Provider retries are bounded and provider-specific, so reconcile gaps rather than waiting indefinitely.
- Providers need durable outboxes, per-endpoint schedules and isolation from slow customers.

## Further reading
- [Stripe docs: Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks)
- [GitHub docs: Best practices for using webhooks](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/best-practices-for-using-webhooks)
- [Standard Webhooks specification](https://github.com/standard-webhooks/standard-webhooks/blob/main/spec/standard-webhooks.md)

questions.prompt: You're consuming Stripe-style payment webhooks with bounded retries and possible duplicates. Which practices should you adopt? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verify the signature, persist the event to a queue, return 200 immediately, then process asynchronously
options.explanation: Correct. Fast acknowledgement avoids provider timeouts (and the duplicate retries they cause), and your downstream outages don't turn into webhook failures.

options.text: Deduplicate on the authenticated event id, in the same transaction as the local database side effect
options.explanation: Correct. Retries can produce duplicates even though bounded retries cannot guarantee delivery. Doing the dedupe insert and the business update atomically prevents a crash between them leaving things inconsistent.

options.text: Assume events arrive in the order they were created
options.explanation: Wrong. Providers such as Stripe explicitly don't guarantee order. Retries and parallel delivery mean `updated` can arrive before `created`.

options.text: Periodically reconcile against the provider's events or objects API
options.explanation: Correct. If your endpoint was down beyond the retry window (Stripe retries for up to 3 days), reconciliation catches missed events. Webhooks are a notification, not your only source of truth.

options.text: Return 500 for event types you don't handle so the provider stops sending them
options.explanation: Wrong. A 5xx tells the provider delivery *failed*, so it retries for days and may eventually disable your endpoint. Return 2xx for events you ignore, and disable their delivery in the provider's settings.

questions.workedExample:
Check each against the delivery model (duplicate-capable, unordered, bounded retries on non-2xx; eventual delivery is not guaranteed):

1. Ack fast + async: avoids timeouts. ✔
2. Dedupe atomically: handles duplicate delivery. ✔
3. Assume order: contradicts 'unordered'. ✘
4. Reconcile: covers deliveries lost beyond the retry window. ✔
5. 500 for unhandled: causes days of retries. ✘

questions.prompt: You run a webhook delivery platform. One large customer's endpoint starts responding in 25 s (timeouts at 30 s). Soon, webhooks for **all** customers are delayed by minutes. What's the most likely design flaw?

options.text: The HMAC signatures are too slow to compute
options.explanation: The scenario points to workers held by slow network responses. Measure cryptographic costs on the actual hardware; no HMAC benchmark is supplied here.

options.text: All customers share one pool of delivery workers, so slow deliveries to one endpoint tie up workers and starve everyone else
options.explanation: Correct. If the large customer generates many events and each takes 25 s, workers sit blocked on that endpoint. Fix with per-endpoint concurrency limits, separate queues per customer (or per shard), shorter timeouts, and circuit breakers that back off failing endpoints.

options.text: Exponential backoff is too aggressive
options.explanation: Backoff slows retries to the failing endpoint. It reduces pressure rather than causing delays for other customers.

options.text: Events are signed with the wrong secret
options.explanation: A wrong secret would cause the customer's verification to fail (and return 4xx), not make deliveries to other customers slow.

questions.workedExample: Slow deliveries hold shared workers for longer. If one customer consumes the pool, other customers wait despite having healthy endpoints. Apply per-endpoint concurrency bounds and queue isolation, with appropriate timeouts and backoff. Provisioning more workers alone does not establish isolation or bound a single customer’s future demand.

questions.prompt: You're building webhook delivery for your own SaaS platform. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change that caused it, and deliver from there
options.explanation: Correct. If the transaction commits, the event is guaranteed to exist; if it rolls back, no phantom event is sent.

options.text: Send the webhook synchronously inside the API request that caused the event
options.explanation: Unsound. A slow or down customer endpoint then slows or fails *your* API request, and a crash between commit and send loses the event.

options.text: Give each customer endpoint its own queue or concurrency limit, so one slow endpoint can't starve the rest
options.explanation: Correct. Isolation stops one customer's 25-second timeouts from tying up the shared worker pool.

options.text: Retry failed deliveries every second, indefinitely
options.explanation: Unsound. That hammers an endpoint that's already struggling and never gives up. Use exponential backoff over hours to days, then disable and notify.

options.text: Sign `id.timestamp.body` with a per-endpoint secret, and offer a `GET /events` API for reconciliation
options.explanation: Correct. Signing the id and timestamp lets consumers reject forgeries and stale replays; the events API lets them recover anything they missed.

questions.workedExample:
Check each choice against the provider's three jobs: **durably record** events, **isolate customer workloads**, and **let consumers verify and recover**.

| Choice | Lose? | Isolate? | Verify? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Outbox | Safe | - | - |
| Sync send | Loses | Couples | - |
| Per-endpoint queues | - | Yes | - |
| Retry every 1 s | - | Hurts | - |
| Sign + events API | - | - | Yes |

The outbox is the same transactional pattern as in the idempotency lesson, applied to outgoing events.

questions.prompt: Your webhook endpoint recovers from an outage before the provider’s next scheduled retry. Why should you reconcile missed events instead of simply waiting?

options.text: The provider always detects recovery and delivers immediately.
options.explanation: A scheduled retry system need not know when the endpoint recovers.

options.text: Every missed event is permanently lost at the first failure.
options.explanation: Providers may retain retries or expose an events API.

options.text: Recovery does not move the next retry forward, and a bounded retry window can expire.
options.explanation: Correct. Reconciliation or supported redelivery can recover state sooner and cover missed attempts.

options.text: A valid HMAC proves that no deliveries were missed.
options.explanation: Authentication says nothing about completeness of delivery.

questions.workedExample: An endpoint can be healthy while a retry remains scheduled for much later. It can also have been unavailable longer than the provider retains retries. Fetch authoritative events or current objects, process them idempotently and use supported redelivery where appropriate.

lessons.title: Out-of-order webhooks and current state
lessons.summary: Reject stale object versions or serialise authoritative refreshes when notifications arrive out of order.
lessons.body:
## Problem 4: ordering

Webhooks can arrive **out of order**. Retries, parallel workers and network variation mean `subscription.updated` can arrive before `subscription.created`. Stripe explicitly says it doesn't guarantee delivery order.

Strategies:

- **Use trustworthy per-object versions.** Atomically apply only newer versions. Timestamps work only if their ordering and tie-breaking are reliable for that object; event creation time is not automatically an object version.
- **Treat events as hints ("thin events").** On any event for object X, call `GET /objects/X` to fetch its current state. This avoids applying stale event payloads, but concurrent fetches can still complete out of order. Serialize refreshes per object or apply a trustworthy version check when storing the fetched state. Stripe's newer "thin" events take this approach: the payload contains little more than the id.
- **Strict per-key ordering** on the provider side (one in-flight delivery per object with ordered retries) trades throughput and head-of-line blocking for ordering. A consumer that acknowledges before asynchronous processing must preserve order there too.

| Problem | Consumer fix |
|---|---|
| Fake events | Verify HMAC (raw body) |
| Replays | Signed timestamp + tolerance |
| Duplicates | Dedupe on event id |
| Timeouts | Ack fast, process async |
| Out of order | Version check or re-fetch |
| Missed events | Reconcile via events API |

## Key takeaways
- Retries and parallel delivery can reverse event arrival order.
- Apply trustworthy newer object versions atomically; event timestamps are not automatically versions.
- Treat thin events as refresh hints and protect concurrent fetch completion order.
- Strict per-key ordering trades throughput for blocking and must continue through asynchronous processing.

## Further reading
- [Stripe docs: Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks)

questions.prompt: You receive `subscription.updated` (plan = Pro, version 7) and then, due to a retry, an older `subscription.updated` (plan = Basic, version 5). Your handler simply writes the event's plan to the database. What ends up stored, and what's the most robust fix?

options.text: Pro; webhooks are always delivered in order
options.explanation: They aren't. Retries of earlier failed deliveries commonly arrive after newer events.

options.text: Pro; databases reject older writes automatically
options.explanation: A plain `UPDATE` has no notion of event age. It overwrites whatever is there unless you add a condition.

options.text: Basic. Fix: on any subscription event, re-fetch the subscription's current state from the provider's API (or only apply events with a higher version than stored)
options.explanation: Correct. The stale event overwrote newer data. Treating events as hints helps, but concurrent refresh responses can still finish out of order; serialize refreshes per object or guard the stored version. An atomic version check (`WHERE version < 5` fails, so skip) is the cheaper alternative.

options.text: Basic. Fix: process webhooks with a single thread
options.explanation: A single thread processes events in *arrival* order, but arrival order is already wrong here. Serialising doesn't fix out-of-order delivery.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline:

```
arrive 1: v7 plan=Pro   -> store Pro
arrive 2: v5 plan=Basic -> store Basic
```

Customer paid for Pro but now has Basic. Fixes:

**Version guard**

```sql
-- Ignore equal or older object
-- versions.
UPDATE subs SET plan=$p, ver=$v
WHERE id=$id AND ver < $v
```

stored version 7 < incoming version 5 is false → 0 rows → ignored.

**Re-fetch** (thin-event style)

On any event for `sub_123`, call `GET /subscriptions/sub_123` and store the result. Serialize these refreshes per object or use a trustworthy version check when storing fetched state; otherwise an older fetch can overwrite a newer one.

lessons.title: API gateways and backends for frontends
lessons.summary: Separate edge policy from client-specific response shaping and keep business rules in core services.
lessons.body:
## API gateways

As systems grow into dozens of services, you don't want every service to re-implement auth, rate limiting and TLS. An **API gateway** is a reverse proxy that handles these cross-cutting concerns at the edge.

```
   clients
      |
+------------+
| API gateway|  TLS, auth,
|            |  rate limit,
+------------+  routing, logs
  |    |    |
 svc  svc  svc
```

Typical responsibilities:

- **Routing**: `/orders/*` to the orders service, `/v2/*` to new deployments, canary splits.
- **Authentication**: validate JWTs or API keys, then pass a verified identity downstream.
- **Rate limiting and quotas** per API key or plan.
- **TLS termination**, request size limits, WAF rules.
- **Observability**: request ids, access logs, metrics, tracing headers.
- **Transformation**: header injection, protocol translation (REST to gRPC).

Examples: Kong, AWS API Gateway, Apigee, Azure API Management, Envoy-based gateways. Load balancing itself is covered in the networking module; a gateway is an L7 proxy with API-aware features layered on top.

> [!warning] Don't turn the gateway into a monolith
> Keep business logic out. Once the gateway starts aggregating responses, applying domain rules and knowing about order states, every team's change has to go through it, and it becomes the bottleneck you split your monolith to escape.

Also remember the gateway is on every request's path: it must be horizontally scaled, highly available and fast. A gateway that adds 30 ms to every call becomes a big chunk of your latency budget.

## Backend-for-frontend (BFF)

Different clients need different things. The iOS app wants small payloads tuned for a phone screen. The web app shows richer pages. A partner integration wants stable, generic resources. One general-purpose API ends up serving all of them badly.

The **backend-for-frontend** pattern, popularised by Sam Newman and based on work at SoundCloud, can give each distinct client experience its **own** thin backend, owned by the team that builds that frontend.

```
 iOS     Android    Web
  |        |         |
+----+  +----+   +-----+
|BFF |  |BFF |   | BFF |
|mob |  |mob |   | web |
+----+  +----+   +-----+
   \       |       /
  +----------------+
  |  core services |
  +----------------+
```

What a BFF does:

- **Aggregates** several downstream calls into one response shaped for a specific screen, cutting mobile round trips.
- **Trims** payloads to what that client needs.
- **Handles client-specific concerns**: for browsers, it can hold OAuth tokens server-side and give the browser only an `HttpOnly` session cookie (the "token handler" pattern), keeping tokens out of JavaScript.
- **Evolves with its frontend**, so the mobile team can ship a new screen without waiting for a core-services change.

Trade-offs:

- **Duplication** across BFFs (two mobile BFFs often converge). Share libraries, or merge them if the clients are near-identical.
- **More services to run.**
- Like the gateway, keep **domain logic in core services**. A BFF should orchestrate and shape, not decide business rules.

GraphQL can be an alternative or a complement: clients select response fields through a shared GraphQL schema. Client-specific authentication, aggregation policy and ownership may still justify BFFs.

## Gateway vs BFF

| | API gateway | BFF |
|---|---|---|
| Count | One (or few) | One per client type |
| Owner | Platform team | Frontend team |
| Focus | Cross-cutting | Client-specific shape |
| Logic | Policy only | Aggregation |

They usually coexist: the gateway handles TLS, auth and rate limits at the edge, then routes to the right BFF.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Reception and department assistants
> **How it maps:** Reception applies common entry rules and directs visitors. A department assistant gathers the information that department needs. This resembles an API gateway and a client-specific BFF.
>
> **Where it stops:** The comparison does not decide deployment topology or authorisation scope. Core services still enforce their domain rules and object access checks.

## Key takeaways
- Gateways centralise routing, identity checks, limits, TLS and observability.
- A BFF is owned with its frontend and aggregates or trims responses for that experience.
- Gateways and BFFs both need operational capacity and clear domain boundaries.
- GraphQL and BFFs can complement each other; neither removes client-specific ownership decisions.

questions.prompt: Your mobile home screen needs data from 5 services, and on 4G each round trip costs ~150 ms. The web app needs a very different shape from the same services. The mobile team waits weeks for core teams to change endpoints. Which pattern best addresses this?

options.text: Put the aggregation logic for every client in the shared API gateway
options.explanation: This turns the gateway into a monolith owned by a platform team. Every client change now queues behind that team, which is the same bottleneck in a new place.

options.text: Have the mobile app call all 5 services directly in parallel
options.explanation: Parallel calls help latency, but the app still downloads 5 over-fetched payloads, and still depends on core teams for any shape change.

options.text: A backend-for-frontend per client type (mobile BFF, web BFF), owned by each frontend team, that aggregates and shapes responses
options.explanation: Correct. The mobile BFF makes the 5 calls over the fast data-centre network and returns one trimmed payload; the mobile team owns it, so they can change it without waiting for core teams.

options.text: Add a version number to each core service's API
options.explanation: Versioning manages breaking changes, but doesn't reduce round trips or let the mobile team shape responses themselves.

questions.workedExample:
Illustrative latency model (assumed payload sizes and internal latency; excludes processing and transfer time):

- **Direct, sequential**: 5 × 150 ms = 750 ms.
- **Direct, parallel**: ~150 ms, but 5 payloads (say 5 × 40 KB = 200 KB) over 4G.
- **BFF**: 1 × 150 ms on 4G + 5 parallel calls in the data centre at ~5 ms each, returning one 15 KB payload.

Ownership matters as much as latency: the BFF lives with the mobile team, so a new screen means changing their own service, not filing tickets with five other teams.

questions.prompt: The platform team proposes adding a rule to the API gateway: "if a customer has more than 5 past orders, add a 10% loyalty discount to `POST /checkout` requests". It would ship faster than changing the checkout service. What's the strongest objection?

options.text: It's business logic. Putting domain rules in the gateway couples every team to it, makes it the bottleneck for changes, and hides pricing rules from the service that owns checkout
options.explanation: Correct. Gateways should handle cross-cutting policy (auth, rate limits, routing, TLS). Once they apply domain rules, they become the shared monolith you split up to escape.

options.text: Gateways can't modify request bodies
options.explanation: Many gateways can transform requests. The issue isn't capability; it's that this logic doesn't belong there.

options.text: It would break TLS termination
options.explanation: TLS is terminated before the gateway sees the request either way. The discount rule has nothing to do with TLS.

options.text: Gateways can only route by URL path
options.explanation: Modern gateways route on headers, methods, weights and more. Again, capability isn't the problem.

questions.workedExample:
Ask of any proposed gateway feature: *is this true for every API, or is it a rule about this domain?*

| Feature | Cross-cutting? | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Validate JWT | Yes | Gateway |
| 1,000 req/min per key | Yes | Gateway |
| Route `/orders/*` | Yes | Gateway |
| Loyalty discount | No | Checkout service |

The discount also needs order history, which means the gateway calling a database or service on the hot path of a single endpoint. That adds latency to the one component every request already passes through.
